PROVIDENCE, RI — As demand grows for skilled engineers and technicians to power Rhode Island's advanced manufacturing, marine, and clean energy sectors, U.S. Senators Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse and Representatives Seth Magaziner (RI-02) and Gabe Amo (RI-01) announced $4,619,389 of federal funding awarded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to the University of Rhode Island, in partnership with the Community College of Rhode Island, to support scholarships for high-achieving, low-income students pursuing degrees in engineering and engineering technology.

The program stands to benefit workforce development across multiple sectors, including Rhode Island's blue economy and advanced manufacturing industry. It is set to begin in January.

“This is a wise investment in individuals, Rhode Island’s workforce, and American science and engineering expertise, which is increasingly critical for our economy and national defense. Helping smart kids afford an engineering degree is a win-win. They get the skills that put them on promising career pathways for critical, in-demand jobs and America stays competitive,” said Senator Reed.

“Rhode Island’s institutions of higher education are on the leading edge of STEM innovation and help power the Ocean State’s economic competitiveness,” said Senator Whitehouse. “This federal funding will create opportunities for deserving Rhode Island students to follow their dreams at URI and CCRI.”

"Rhode Island needs more engineers, and this funding will help make sure that talented students across our state have a real shot at that career, no matter their financial background," said Rep. Magaziner. "I am proud to work alongside the Rhode Island Congressional delegation to deliver the funding needed to support workforce training here in the Ocean State.”

"I'm proud to work alongside our Rhode Island Delegation to expand opportunity for talented students at the University of Rhode Island and the Community College of Rhode Island,” said Rep. Amo. "This federal funding will remove financial barriers for students and set them up for good-paying engineering jobs that will power Rhode Island's economy of tomorrow."

“This project will help reduce the financial burden for students pursuing an engineering degree and, ultimately, the amount of debt they may carry after graduation,” said Vinka Craver, associate dean for research at URI’s College of Engineering and Principal Investigator on the NSF grant. “But the program goes beyond financial support. From their first year, students will have access to faculty and industry mentors and opportunities to participate in internships and capstone projects, helping them build the experience and connections they need to be better prepared for their professional careers.”

"Cost should never stand between a talented student and their future. This grant makes that future possible for Rhode Island students pursuing degrees in engineering and engineering technology. Through our partnership with URI, we're building a talent pipeline into the advanced manufacturing, marine, and clean energy jobs that are shaping Rhode Island's economy,” said Rosemary A. Costigan, Ph.D., RN, president of the Community College of Rhode Island. “I'm grateful to Senators Reed and Whitehouse and Representatives Magaziner and Amo for their continued investment in our students and our state's workforce future."

A total of 116 scholars pursuing associate's degrees in engineering technology at CCRI and bachelor's degrees in engineering and engineering technology at URI will receive scholarships for up to five years, along with mentoring and other support services designed to improve retention and graduation rates.

The award is administered by the National Science Foundation (NSF) as part of NSF's Scholarships in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (S-STEM) program, which supports the retention and graduation of academically talented, low-income students with demonstrated financial need in STEM fields. The project, entitled "Collaborative Research: Advancing Pathways through a Multi-Institutional Consortium for Engineering Education and Workforce Development," will be evaluated on an ongoing basis to help identify effective strategies for supporting low-income students in STEM.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Rep. George Whitesides (CA-27) introduced the Stop Predator Dumping Act, legislation that would protect rural communities by mandating a new placement framework for Sexually Violent Predators (SVPs). The bill aims to stop communities from being disproportionately impacted by repeated SVP placements, an issue that has historically burdened areas like the Antelope Valley.

“For too long, communities like the Antelope Valley have been treated as dumping grounds for Sexually Violent Predators, while other areas share none of the burden,” said Rep. Whitesides. “This legislation ensures a fair and transparent approach to SVP placements nationwide. We must prioritize the safety of our communities and ensure no single region is forced to bear this burden alone.”

The current approach to SVP placements in many states has allowed for the concentration of offenders in specific regions, straining local resources and impacting community safety. The Stop Predator Dumping Act would overhaul this system by mandating that states adopt a strict placement framework.

Additionally, the legislation directs the Department of Justice (DOJ) to study, compile, and promulgate best practices to states, ensuring that areas like the Antelope Valley do not bear the brunt of these placements through repeated dumping. To help states execute these new guidelines, the bill establishes a federal grant program to fund the implementation of these best practices at the state and local levels.

Specifically, the Stop Predator Dumping Act would:

Establish strict proximity limits, prohibiting any offenders from being placed within 10 miles of each other.

Prohibit repeated placements in a single county subdivision until all other subdivisions within that county have received a placement.

Implement a strict county cap for counties with populations over 1 million people, ensuring that no single county governing district (such as the Antelope Valley at-large) can house more than 25% of the total SVPs in a county like Los Angeles.

Require the DOJ to study and promulgate best practices to states regarding SVP placements to prevent disproportionate dumping in communities.

Create a new federal grant program to assist states in implementing and carrying out these best practices.

###
title: Rep. Whitesides Introduces Legislation to Protect the Antelope Valley by Stopping the Dumping of Sexually Violent Predators in Rural Communities

BERKELEY, CA – Congresswoman Lateefah Simon (D-CA-12) recently secured $850,000 in federal Community Project Funding (CPF) for the City of Berkeley to design new public open spaces along Adeline Street, including a new main plaza adjacent to the future transit-oriented development on the west parking lot of the Ashby Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) station.

The federal funding will support the design of a vibrant community plaza and other public open spaces for South Berkeley that will complement new housing, including affordable housing, as well as new commercial and community spaces. The project will also improve access to the BART station, including pedestrian and ADA access.

Last week, the Congresswoman announced the funding alongside Mayor of Berkeley Adena Ishii, Berkeley City Councilmember Ben Bartlett, BART General Manager Bob Powers, BART Board Director Barnali Ghosh, and community partners.

As a disability and transit justice advocate, Congresswoman Simon has long to create vibrant communities where there is equitable housing development near affordable and accessible transit. Additionally, during her time as BART Board President, she led on redeveloping the Ashby BART station. In Congress, Congresswoman Simon has also introduced the Connecting Communities Through Transit Planning Act, which would make permanent and expand the Pilot Program for Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) Planning to support housing projects near new or existing transit corridors.

“I helped jumpstart and plan the Ashby BART station transit-oriented development project when I served as BART Board President – and I am extremely proud to now secure nearly a million in federal funding to further the process on a new plaza that will complement the Ashby BART transit-oriented development,” said Congresswoman Simon. “Transforming this public space along Adeline Street into a plaza where people can live, work, and play near affordable and accessible transit will be game changing and create more vibrant, connected communities that succeed both economically and culturally.”

“I'm proud to join Congresswoman Simon in announcing this $850,000 investment in South Berkeley. It's one of our most diverse communities, and it's been underinvested in and underserved for too long. Now, we're changing that,” said Mayor of Berkeley, Adena Ishii. “This project looks to create a future of greater economic opportunity and better access for people with disabilities, complementing the new housing already planned for Adeline Street.”

This Community Project Funding (CPF) is a part of the $11.2 million dollars that Congresswoman Simon secured for 15 projects across the East Bay in Fiscal Year 2026. House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force Submits Amicus Brief Defending Watergate-Era Law Protecting the Public’s Right to Presidential Records
Washington, D.C. — Today, House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force mobilized in support of a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s unlawful attempt to erase a nearly 50-year-old, bipartisan safeguard for presidential records. The Members of Congress filed an amicus brief in American Historical Association v. Trump, a lawsuit brought by historians seeking to preserve White House papers and electronic messages for the American people.
This action follows the fundamentally flawed April 2026 opinion from the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel which concluded the Presidential Records Act (PRA), a post-Watergate law designed to promote government transparency, is unconstitutional. It marks yet another attempt by the Trump administration to evade restraints on presidential power.
The brief was led by Task Force Co-Chairs Assistant Leader Joe Neguse, Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, and Oversight Ranking Member Robert Garcia, as well as House Administration Ranking Member Joe Morelle. It was signed by 106 House Democrats.
“Each of Congress’s primary purposes for the [Presidential Records Act] was designed to further the public interest,” argued the amicus curiae. “Congress resolved the question of who owns official presidential records in favor of the public; ensured official presidential records would be preserved for and accessible by the public; and facilitated the success of each new President for the benefit of the public the President is popularly elected to serve. If compliance with the Act lapsed, it is the public who would be harmed. And that harm would be both immediate and irreparable.”
In their filing, the Members of Congress clearly convey the constitutional authority on which the PRA rests and how the long-standing law serves vital public purposes: preserving our history, ensuring government continuity, and protecting the public’s access to presidential records. They argue that Congress carefully balanced those interests with legitimate presidential prerogatives, and that President Trump’s effort to dismantle this safeguard altogether threatens the public’s right to preserve and understand the nation’s past.
Click HERE to view the full brief.
Look below to see what the leading lawmakers had to say about the matter:
“The Presidential Records Act has protected a basic democratic principle for nearly a half-century: all official records of the White House belong to the American people. Now, as part of its continuing desperate attempt to cover up all the outrageous corruption, inside dealing, bribery and incompetence in what remains of the White House, Trump’s servile Justice Department is trying to give ‘the most transparent President ever’ a way to conceal and destroy official records, memos and correspondence establishing the actions of his administration. I’m proud to stand with my colleagues in urging the court to remind the President and his Administration that, in America, public records belong to the public and public officials serve the American people, not the other way around,” said Ranking Member Raskin.
“Donald Trump continuously abuses the office of the presidency to erode transparency and evade accountability. His latest attempt to erase a decades-old, bipartisan law establishing that presidential records belong to the American public should not just be deemed unlawful — but it should be viewed through the deeply disturbing lens of an administration seeking to rewrite the history of its failed presidency,” said Assistant Leader Joe Neguse.
"Donald Trump wants to shred any and all evidence of his countless corrupt actions, and that's why his DOJ is helping him ignore the Presidential Records Act. President Trump's attempts to play king and duck accountability will not work. We're fighting this in court and will continue defending transparency for the American people," said Ranking Member Garcia.
“The Presidential Records Act protects the American public’s right to their own history. It’s a critical anticorruption and transparency law that preserves access to important records and promotes good government. By illegally attempting to dismantle it, Donald Trump is undermining these protections and avoiding responsibility for a corrupt administration determined to eliminate any restraints on presidential power. We won't let that happen," said Ranking Member Morelle.
Background
The Litigation Task Force launched in the first month that followed President Donald Trump’s chaotic return to office. We immediately set out to push back against an administration showing no respect for the Constitution or rule of law—and we haven’t stopped since. Our first amicus brief, filed in February 2025, defended American consumers from predatory lenders and other bad actors and helped persuade a federal judge to block efforts to dismantle the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
Since then, the Task Force has directly responded to a myriad of other unlawful directives issued by the Trump administration, including simultaneously filing a court motion challenging the legitimacy of the president’s corrupt attempt to “settle” his lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — an agency he oversees — in exchange for the creation of a $1.7 billion slush fund for political allies.
For more information on the Litigation Task Force’s efforts to protect Americans against the unlawful actions of the Trump administration, visit litigationandresponse.house.gov.
title: House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force Submits Amicus Brief Defending Watergate-Era Law Protecting the Public’s Right to Presidential Records

DOVER, Del. — Today, U.S. Representative Sarah McBride and Lt. Governor Kyle Evans Gay (both D-Del.) brought together advocates, childcare providers, and local leaders for a conversation at Delaware State University on lowering childcare costs, expanding access to care, and strengthening Delaware’s childcare workforce.

Rep. McBride was recently selected by House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries to co-lead the House Democratic Caregiving Working Group, which is charged with helping develop the House Democratic Caucus’s legislative agenda on caregiving. Today’s discussion further informs that work, bringing the experiences and priorities of Delaware families and childcare providers directly into creating bold federal solutions to caregiving challenges facing families in the First State and across the country.

“Childcare costs are increasingly unaffordable for working families in Delaware and across the country,” said Rep. McBride. “Access to affordable, reliable childcare must be at the center of our economic agenda at both the federal and state levels. Today’s conversation brought together providers, advocates, and local leaders to talk about what it will take to lower costs for families, expand access to care, and recruit and retain the childcare workers our communities need. As we develop a caregiving agenda for the next Congress, I’m going to make sure the voices and experiences of Delawareans are front and center.”

The discussion focused on four key challenges facing Delaware families and childcare providers: affordability for families; access to and availability of care; financial, operational, and workforce pressures facing providers; as well as state and federal policies that could help address those challenges. Participants also discussed gaps in infant care, care during nontraditional hours, rural childcare, and care for children with disabilities, as well as barriers providers face in recruiting and retaining workers and expanding capacity to meet demand.

“For too long, we have approached early childhood education in Delaware as a collection of individual programs — each with its own funding stream, requirements, eligibility rules, and priorities. But parents don't experience government that way. Educators don’t. And children certainly don’t,” said Lt. Governor Kyle Evans Gay. “We have an opportunity right now to think differently — to move from fragmented programs toward an aligned and coordinated system with sustainable investments. We have the opportunity to design a system around the people that we serve. As Chair of the IRMC, I am committed to that work—and to making sure the we have the honest conversations about governance, financing, coordination, and accountability that this moment requires so that our youngest Delawareans have access to the education and care they need.”

Affordability was a central focus throughout the conversation as families continue to face high childcare costs. According to a recent report, the national average annual price of center-based infant care was $15,570. In Delaware, families are paying approximately $17,252 per year for center-based infant care.

Joining Rep. McBride and Lt. Governor Evans Gay were representatives from:

Child Care for Every Family Network

Delaware Association for the Education of Young Children

YMCA of Delaware

Delaware State Education Association

Delaware State University's Early Childhood Center

Delaware Department of Education

Delaware Department of Health and Social Services

Representatives shared concerns about workforce infrastructure and the increasing costs of providing care, as well as squeezed bottom lines across the board. Each spoke about challenges facing the affordability of childcare — reinforcing the broad effects across every aspect of the economy and workforce — and shared invaluable perspectives about the way families are navigating childcare access and costs across Delaware.

Rep. McBride has long worked to strengthen support for working families. In Congress, she is a cosponsor of the Child Care for Every Community Act, which would create a universal childcare program, and the American Family Act, which would increase the value of a monthly Child Tax Credit.

While serving as a Delaware State Senator, Rep. McBride passed the Healthy Delaware Families Act with bipartisan support, providing paid family and medical leave to workers across the state. In Congress, she has continued to lead on strengthening the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and expanding paid leave nationwide. She has introduced legislation including the FAIR Leave Act, the Flexible Leave Act, and is an original cosponsor of the FAMILY Act, helping ensure workers and their families can access leave when they need it most.

Photos from the event can be found here.

Washington, D.C. — Rep. Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, wrote to 40 agencies and the National Archives and Records Administration, reminding them of their legal responsibility to preserve records under the Federal Records Act, including preserving communications on apps like Signal.
“President Trump wants to delete evidence of his countless corrupt acts and hide his wrongdoing from the American people. We are fighting back in court and we will not let him cover his tracks,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.
Congress enacted the Federal Records Act (FRA) in 1950 following recommendations of the Hoover Commission to ensure that federal agencies properly create, preserve, and manage records documenting the work and decisions of the federal government. Congress enacted the Presidential Records Act (PRA) and in the direct aftermath of Watergate to make sure the records of the White House are not destroyed and may be accessed by the public.
Today, Rep. Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Assistant Leader Joe Neguse, Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Committee on the Judiciary, and Rep. Joe Morelle, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Administration, also led Members of Congress in filing an amicus brief defending the PRA against the Trump Administration’s effort to gut the law by declaring it unconstitutional.
The Oversight Committee has primary jurisdiction over the FRA and PRA.

PROVIDENCE, RI — As demand grows for skilled engineers and technicians to power Rhode Island's advanced manufacturing, marine, and clean energy sectors, U.S. Senators Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse and Representatives Seth Magaziner (RI-02) and Gabe Amo (RI-01) announced $4,619,389 of federal funding awarded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to the University of Rhode Island, in partnership with the Community College of Rhode Island, to support scholarships for high-achieving, low-income students pursuing degrees in engineering and engineering technology.

The program stands to benefit workforce development across multiple sectors, including Rhode Island's blue economy and advanced manufacturing industry. It is set to begin in January.

“This is a wise investment in individuals, Rhode Island’s workforce, and American science and engineering expertise, which is increasingly critical for our economy and national defense. Helping smart kids afford an engineering degree is a win-win. They get the skills that put them on promising career pathways for critical, in-demand jobs and America stays competitive,” said Senator Reed.

“Rhode Island’s institutions of higher education are on the leading edge of STEM innovation and help power the Ocean State’s economic competitiveness,” said Senator Whitehouse. “This federal funding will create opportunities for deserving Rhode Island students to follow their dreams at URI and CCRI.”

"Rhode Island needs more engineers, and this funding will help make sure that talented students across our state have a real shot at that career, no matter their financial background," said Rep. Magaziner. "I am proud to work alongside the Rhode Island Congressional delegation to deliver the funding needed to support workforce training here in the Ocean State.”

"I'm proud to work alongside our Rhode Island Delegation to expand opportunity for talented students at the University of Rhode Island and the Community College of Rhode Island,” said Rep. Amo. "This federal funding will remove financial barriers for students and set them up for good-paying engineering jobs that will power Rhode Island's economy of tomorrow."

“This project will help reduce the financial burden for students pursuing an engineering degree and, ultimately, the amount of debt they may carry after graduation,” said Vinka Craver, associate dean for research at URI’s College of Engineering and Principal Investigator on the NSF grant. “But the program goes beyond financial support. From their first year, students will have access to faculty and industry mentors and opportunities to participate in internships and capstone projects, helping them build the experience and connections they need to be better prepared for their professional careers.”

"Cost should never stand between a talented student and their future. This grant makes that future possible for Rhode Island students pursuing degrees in engineering and engineering technology. Through our partnership with URI, we're building a talent pipeline into the advanced manufacturing, marine, and clean energy jobs that are shaping Rhode Island's economy,” said Rosemary A. Costigan, Ph.D., RN, president of the Community College of Rhode Island. “I'm grateful to Senators Reed and Whitehouse and Representatives Magaziner and Amo for their continued investment in our students and our state's workforce future."

A total of 116 scholars pursuing associate's degrees in engineering technology at CCRI and bachelor's degrees in engineering and engineering technology at URI will receive scholarships for up to five years, along with mentoring and other support services designed to improve retention and graduation rates.

The award is administered by the National Science Foundation (NSF) as part of NSF's Scholarships in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (S-STEM) program, which supports the retention and graduation of academically talented, low-income students with demonstrated financial need in STEM fields. The project, entitled "Collaborative Research: Advancing Pathways through a Multi-Institutional Consortium for Engineering Education and Workforce Development," will be evaluated on an ongoing basis to help identify effective strategies for supporting low-income students in STEM.
title: Rhode Island Congressional Delegation Announces $4.6 Million for URI, CCRI Engineering Workforce Development Program

LOS ANGELES – Congresswoman Luz Rivas (CA-29), co-chair of the STEM Education Caucus, introduced the National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Act of 2026. This bill reauthorizes and modernizes the NSF REU program that has strengthened undergraduate STEM research pathways since 2010.

“Every college student, regardless of their background, deserves the opportunity to engage in STEM research, gain new experiences in the lab, and understand what a potential STEM career could be,” said Congresswoman Rivas. “Opportunities for STEM education experiences should not be limited because of where students go to school. My NSF REU Act expands access to undergraduate research experiences and opportunities to students at minority-serving institutions, community colleges, emerging research institutions, and rural-serving institutions. By strengthening learning opportunities for all students, we can develop a more inclusive and robust STEM workforce that will keep the United States a leader in innovation and technology.”

Background:

The National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Act of 2026 strengthens pathways into STEM careers by prioritizing first-time research participants and students from underrepresented and underserved backgrounds. It expands NSF’s flexibility to support student professional development, mentor training, institutional partnerships, and long-term program evaluation. The legislation reinforces the role of experiential learning in building the STEM workforce, while improving access for students at minority-serving institutions, community colleges, emerging research institutions, and rural-serving institutions.

The NSF REU Act of 2026 would expand access to high-quality undergraduate research experiences and modernize program implementation. Key aspects of this legislation include:

Updates statute to be consistent with NSF’s current implementation of the program;

Provides NSF further flexibility to support undergraduate research, including support for student professional development, faculty supplements to promote community college participation, mentorship training to broaden participation in STEM, and program evaluation and data collection activities;

Clarifies one of the primary intents of the program is to provide first-time research experiences to individuals with limited or no prior experience in STEM or individuals belonging to groups; and

Authorizes an appropriation sum of $100 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2032.
title: Congresswoman Luz Rivas Introduces Bill to Expand Access to Undergraduate Research STEM Programs

San Diego, CA – Today, Rep. Scott Peters convened children’s healthcare and childcare providers to increase awareness of President Trump and HHS Secretary Kennedy’s recent changes that threaten children’s health and wellbeing.

In early August, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced proposed rule changes to Head Start, the nation's early education program for children from low-income families. The move would diminish the program's federal standards and give states and parents more control. A few weeks later, President Trump signed an Executive Order that alters the childhood vaccine schedule and promotes his widely discredited theories about vaccines.

“Back to school season should be an exciting time with new opportunities for kids to learn and grow. But this year, too many parents are forced to worry about the welfare of their children thanks to recent changes from the Trump Administration that threaten their ability to thrive,” said Rep. Peters. “The bottom line is that vaccines keep kids healthy. Head Start ensures every child has an equal opportunity to succeed. Yet from every angle, the Trump Administration’s deregulation efforts set kids up for failure.”

“My message is simple: San Diego Unified will continue following the advice from early childhood medical experts, not politically influenced directives that are in no way based on scientific evidence,” said San Diego Unified School Board Vice President Sabrina Bazzo. “We will keep advocating, alongside Congressman Peters, for full Head Start funding and for vaccine guidance based on data, not ideology. Because we are committed to doing everything in our power to ensure the health and safety of our students.”

“August is back-to-school season for children across California, where they'll spend time learning, playing, and yes, sharing germs,” said Pia Pannaraj, MD, MPH, American Academy of Pediatrics - California Chapter 3 (AAP-CA3). “Non-expert changes to child and adolescent immunization recommendations needlessly put the health and well-being of kids and our communities at risk and create more confusion for parents and caregivers. Here's what I tell parents who come to my clinic with questions: despite the confusing and conflicting information out there, the science hasn't changed. Your pediatricians continue to follow the American Academy of Pediatrics' immunization recommendations because they help keep kids healthy, in the classroom, and ahead of serious, preventable diseases. I encourage parents with questions or concerns to talk with their child's pediatrician.”

“We must keep the promise and build Head Start for what’s next. Fewer rules cannot equal fewer results,” said Damon Carson, General Manager, Neighborhood House Association. “Fewer hours, more turnover, or less experienced staff may save money on one line of a budget, but they create costs somewhere else – for programs, families, and children. And the more resources we have, the earlier we can identify a concern, and the earlier a family can act. Neighborhood House Association staff, families, and partners can submit their own comments on the proposed rules at regulations.gov before the October 6 deadline.”

“The YMCA of San Diego County is dedicated to community well-being and belonging. Alongside critical community partners, we support wholistic family health, which includes access to early care and education,” said Courtney Baltiyskyy, Vice President of Policy & Advocacy, YMCA of San Diego County. “As one of the largest childcare and after school providers in the county, the Y strengthens the broader childcare landscape by supporting families, providers, and employers while advancing systems that work better for everyone. When we think about a thriving San Diego, we know a continuum of quality care and education includes our valuable Head Start programs.”

President Trump's most recent Executive Order on childhood vaccines would stagger the administration of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Public health experts have raised concerns that this creates an increased risk of infection. As kids begin the new school year and during National Immunization Awareness Month, Rep. Peters is calling attention to these changes and encouraging parents to speak out and protect their children.

Simultaneously, the regulatory changes to Head Start would deregulate the program’s student-teacher ratios, staff qualifications, child development screenings, background checks, and safety rules. These rules are not final and are currently in a public comment period until October 6, 2026. San Diegans can share their thoughts on the proposed changes here.

A livestreamed recording of the press conference can be viewed here. Additional photos from the event, courtesy of the office of Rep. Scott Peters, can be viewed here.

title: Rep. Peters and Healthcare, Childcare Providers Denounce Trump Administration’s Threats to Child Welfare

Huffman, Dexter Demand Records from Corporate Sponsors of Freedom 250
Letters to 24 sponsors and partners follow interim report finding the White House turned the nation’s 250th birthday into a fundraising operation for the President
Washington, D.C. – Today, House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) and Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee Ranking Member Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.) sent letters to 24 corporate sponsors and partners of Freedom 250, LLC, demanding documents and communications related to their donations to the entity at the center of the White House’s takeover of the nation’s 250th celebration. 
In the letters, the lawmakers point to the Committee’s July interim report, From Vanity to Insanity: How the White House Cheated the American People out of their 250th Birthday, which “found that the White House hijacked the nation’s semiquincentennial celebration, converting a once-in-a-generation national commemoration into an apparatus for raising and spending money in service of the President’s political ideology and vanity projects. Freedom 250, a wholly owned subsidiary lodged within the National Park Foundation, was created as a new entity to facilitate this takeover.” 
“As a sponsor or partner, your organization possesses documents and information essential to this investigation,” the lawmakers wrote. 
The lawmakers are investigating “whether, how, and to what extent Freedom 250 and those acting in concert with it solicited donations by trading on official access, by misrepresenting the recipient or intended use of funds, or by leveraging donors’ business before the federal government.” They wrote that the inquiry “will inform potential legislation, including to ensure that the hijacking of the semiquincentennial does not become a template for further wrongdoing.”
The letters were sent to corporate sponsors of Freedom250, which include Boeing, Chevron, Deloitte, Exiger, ExxonMobil, iHeartMedia, January AI, John Deere, Lockheed Martin, Mastercard, Mosaic, Northrop Grumman, Oracle, Palantir, Penske, Phorm Energy, RTX, SAP, Scotts Miracle-Gro, Softbank, TikTok, UFC, United Airlines, and United Health Group. 
Read the full request to one of Freedom250’s corporate sponsors here. 
Background 
The Committee’s July interim report found that when the congressionally chartered, nonpartisan America250 Commission refused to bend to the President’s demands, the White House built a replacement, Freedom 250, LLC, and declared it the central platform for the national celebration. The White House lodged that entity inside the National Park Foundation so it could draw on the credibility and donor relationships of a public charity while operating outside the transparency rules Congress wrote into law for the commission. 
The Committee’s July 2 report found that Freedom 250 circulated sponsorship packages starting at $500,000 and climbing above $10 million, backed by the promise of a photo opportunity with President Trump. Its CEO solicited foreign governments and corporations at Davos. Fundraisers appear to have misled donors who meant to give to America250, handing them Freedom 250’s banking information instead, conduct the report found could amount to wire fraud. The report also found that Freedom 250 harvested Americans’ personal data, routing event registration through Campaign Nucleus, the firm founded by Trump campaign operative Brad Parscale, which scores visitors with artificial intelligence to target “persuadable voters.” 
The report concluded that Freedom 250 has created a blueprint for corruption, not a one-time abuse, pointing to the Department of Agriculture, where the administration steered companies with business before the government to donate through a conservation charity into a fund the Secretary controls.

Washington, D.C. – Congresswoman Shontel Brown (OH-11) and U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) are urging the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to investigate the Department of Transportation’s (DOT) ongoing failure to protect passenger privacy using its authority to regulate the practices of commercial airlines and ticket agents. Brown serves as Ranking Member of the House Oversight Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation.

A copy of the full letter sent to the GAO is available here.

For over four decades, the DOT has held exclusive jurisdiction over safeguarding passenger data; nonetheless, a Congressional Research Service evaluation reveals the agency has failed to execute a single privacy enforcement measure, despite severe breaches impacting hundreds of millions of commuters. This prolonged inaction exposes confidential travel information to corporate data mining, federal monitoring, and security risks from hostile foreign nations.

“DOT’s abdication of its role as a privacy regulator has left the sensitive personal information of hundreds of millions of Americans exposed to corporate exploitation, warrantless government surveillance, and warrantless seizure of money and other property,” the lawmakers wrote in letter to Acting Comptroller General Orice W. Brown. “In addition to harming the public, DOT’s regulatory inaction also potentially threatens national security. Travel data held by airlines and travel agencies may be of interest to foreign adversaries, who could exploit such information to track U.S. military, diplomatic, and other U.S. government personnel.”

Historically, DOT has taken a reactive approach to airline privacy, relying on consumer complaints instead of proactively auditing airlines’ privacy practices. In March 2024 Senator Wyden partnered with the DOT to launch a first-ever industry-wide review into the privacy practices of the nation’s 10 largest airlines. More than two years later, DOT has not publicly released its findings or announced any enforcement actions.

The need for stronger DOT oversight is clear. For years, a data broker collectively owned by major U.S. airlines, the Airline Reporting Corporation (ARC) provided federal agencies access to roughly 722 million passenger travel records without warrants or judicial oversight. ARC shut down the program in November 2025, but DHS has since sought a replacement passenger-surveillance system.

Brown and Wyden asked the GAO to launch a comprehensive investigation into the DOT’s systemic failure to fulfill its consumer privacy enforcement responsibilities, by answering the following questions:

Status of the 2024 Airline Privacy Review: Provide a full accounting of the status, findings, and disposition of the industry-wide review launched on March 21, 2024.

Audit of Agency Personnel and Technical Expertise: Identify the exact number of full-time personnel within the OACP currently dedicated exclusively to privacy enforcement, including the number of technologists.

Audit of Interagency Coordination on DEA Informants: Review the interagency coordination between DOT and the Department of Justice (DOJ) over airline employees selling passenger data to the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), including any delays and actions taken to hold airlines accountable.

Agency Response to Widespread Public Scandals: Evaluate whether DOT independently investigated ARC’s sale of passenger records or took action only after congressional and media pressure led to the program’s closure in November 2025.

Structural Nature of the Complaint-Driven Model: Examine why DOT relies on a complaint-driven model instead of routine privacy audits.

Assessment of Insider Threat Mitigation and Data Governance: Evaluate whether the DOT has established guidelines regarding airlines’ protection of Passenger Name Record (PNR) databases against insider threats.

International Data Commitments: Explain how DOT’s domestic privacy enforcement since July 2023 aligns with its commitments to the European Commission under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF).

The lawmakers asked GAO to respond with legislative recommendations to strengthen DOT’s enforcement authority and better protect travelers’ privacy rights.

“If the DOT continues to neglect its domestic regulatory obligations, it risks undermining the integrity of this entire agreement, potentially collapsing transatlantic data flows and destroying vital economic benefits for U.S. companies,” the law makers concluded.

###
title: Brown, Wyden Call for GAO Investigation After DOT Fails to Protect Airline Passenger Data

WASHINGTON, D.C. — This week, Congresswoman Alma S. Adams, Ph.D. (NC-12), and Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) introduced the Black Breastfeeding Week Resolution to recognize the week of August 25, 2026, to August 31, 2026, as “Black Breastfeeding Week.”

According to the CDC, about 80% of Black mothers breastfeed their infants compared to 88% of white mothers, even though breastfeeding is linked to lower risk of short and long-term illness, stronger immune function, and better early childhood development in infants. Black Breastfeeding Week is a time to recognize the disparities Black women face in their ability to meet breastfeeding guidelines, including unequal access to lactation support, workplace accommodations, and quality healthcare.

“The science is clear: breastfeeding improves infant health outcomes, but Black women in America face a breastfeeding disparity,” said Congresswoman Adams, Co-founder and Co-chair of the Black Maternal Health Caucus. “Maternal leave, accessible healthcare, food security, and racial equity in healthcare are all essential supports that Black women need to breastfeed their children — supports that are often not available. That is why breastfeeding is a Black maternal health issue, and it’s one we must address to prevent more of our mothers and children from needlessly losing their lives.”

“Soaring prices are making it harder than ever to feed a family. Breastfeeding is healthier and less costly than formula, yet Black mothers are told to feed their babies formula at far higher rates than other women,” said Congresswoman Watson Coleman, Co-chair of the Caucus on Black Women and Girls. “For generations, racial bias and medical neglect have led to disproportionately worse maternal outcomes for Black women. Breastfeeding support is a major health equity issue and a real hunger issue. All women deserve access to reliable medical advice and competent care to make the best decisions for themselves and their babies.”

The Office of Minority Health found that, in 2024, the rate of infant mortality for Black babies was double the mortality rate of infants nationwide and Black infants were two and a half times as likely to die from sudden infant death syndrome. Meanwhile, the NIH found that breastfeeding reduced the rate of sudden infant death syndrome in 2009, and the CDC recommends breastfeeding as the best source of nutrition for most infants.
title: Reps. Adams, Watson Coleman Introduce Black Breastfeeding Week Resolution

NEWARK, NJ – Today, on a briefing call, Congresswoman LaMonica McIver (NJ-10) and her counsel, Paul Fishman, broke down Wednesday's Third Circuit decision to not dismiss U.S. v. McIver. The decision carries troubling legal and political implications that threaten separation of powers.

McIver and Fishman discussed the complex ruling— the Court ruled to not dismiss the case on two counts and ruled to vacate and remand the third count— the next steps from the court and the legal team, and the broader implications and consequences of the case for democracy. The case, if not dismissed, would set a precedent for extreme ICE impunity, executive branch overreach, and weaponization of the DOJ.

Below are excerpts from the briefing.

Fishman on the stakes of the case

“Let me make something clear. We are not afraid to try this case, and if we try this case…we will win that trial.

[...]

“This is a fight for Congresswoman McIver and every other member of the House of Representatives and the United States Senate who could be targeted by this administration for speaking out, for conducting oversight of the executive branch… [The case is] designed both to chill her and to chill the other members who want to engage in…the same kind of conduct and hold the executive branch responsible for what they're doing.”

McIver on defending and serving her district

“Making sure that my duties as a member representing the 10th district doesn't fall short at all is something that I was very adamant about when [the Trump administration] charged me. I think that's what they hoped for, that it would cripple me in doing my job… But we’ve delivered thousands of dollars in casework and continue to show up on so many different fronts.

“I'm super just grateful for the support I have in my district… That was the reason that took me to Delaney in the first place. The response that I was getting from my community about the things that they heard and saw happening… So I'm going to continue to… show up for them, and protect them, and fight for them because that's what they elected me to do.”

For additional information on the upcoming developments in McIver’s case, please contact Hanna.Rumsey@mail.house.gov.

###
title: ICYMI: McIver and Counsel Paul Fishman Press Call Debriefing Court’s Refusal To Dismiss U.S. v. McIver Case

WASHINGTON — Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), a senior member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, today demanded answers from Attorney General Todd Blanche following reports that a lawyer convicted of hacking election websites joined the Trump Administration’s Civil Rights Division and participated in its election-monitoring operation during Minnesota’s August primary. The reports come as DOJ prepares to deploy as many as 1,000 personnel during the November midterm elections, raising urgent questions about who the Department is entrusting with access to polling locations and voters.

In the letter, Krishnamoorthi writes:

“Reports indicate that David Michael Levin—a Florida attorney who pleaded guilty in 2016 to unauthorized computer intrusions involving two election websites—appears to have joined the Department’s Civil Rights Division and participated in the Department’s monitoring of Minnesota’s August primary. Photographs and video reviewed by reporters reportedly show Mr. Levin standing alongside a Civil Rights Division attorney at a Minneapolis polling location, where a local election judge intervened after the two men positioned themselves too close to the polling place.”

According to Florida investigators, Levin used SQL injection techniques to obtain the login credentials of the Lee County Supervisor of Elections and used those credentials to access the office’s website as an administrator. He also targeted the Florida Division of Elections website. Levin was originally charged with three felonies, ultimately pleaded guilty to two misdemeanors, and served 20 days in jail.

DOJ has not publicly explained Levin’s employment status, his role in the monitoring operation, or how he was selected to participate. Reports have also identified other individuals brought into the Civil Rights Division who have publicly questioned the legitimacy of past elections.

Krishnamoorthi continues:

“These reports raise a fundamental question: What standards is the Department applying when selecting the personnel who will be responsible for protecting Americans’ voting rights?”

The letter follows Krishnamoorthi’s August 19 demand for safeguards against voter intimidation and answers on how DOJ will select, train, and supervise as many as 1,000 election monitors it plans to deploy during the 2026 midterms, nearly twice the size of its 2024 effort.

Krishnamoorthi writes:

“If the reports concerning Mr. Levin are accurate, his presence at a polling location would call that confidence into question. An individual with a documented history of unauthorized access to election systems should not be placed in a position of authority or proximity to voters and election officials without a clear explanation from the Department of the vetting, supervision, and legal authority governing that assignment.”

Krishnamoorthi requested responses to the following questions by September 3, 2026:

Is David Michael Levin currently, or has he previously been, an employee, contractor, detailee, or volunteer of the Civil Rights Division? If so, please identify his position, responsibilities, and dates of service.

What vetting process does the Department require before assigning an individual to election-monitoring duties, including criminal background checks and reviews of an individual’s prior involvement with election systems or election-related activities? Was that process followed in Mr. Levin’s case?

Were Department officials aware of Mr. Levin’s 2016 conviction for unauthorized access to election systems before he participated in the Minneapolis monitoring operation? If so, who approved his participation?

Under what legal authority was Mr. Levin present at the Powderhorn Park polling location? Was he a duly appointed federal election observer, a Civil Rights Division employee, or acting in another capacity?

What training and written guidance are provided to election monitors regarding permissible conduct inside or near polling places, including restrictions designed to prevent voter intimidation and interference with election officials?

What screening criteria will the Department apply to the approximately 1,000 personnel it plans to deploy in November? Will those criteria include an individual’s criminal history, prior conduct involving election systems, and public efforts to undermine confidence in lawful elections?

Will the Department provide Congress with a written description of the vetting, training, supervision, and disciplinary procedures governing its 2026 election-monitoring program before those personnel are deployed?

Krishnamoorthi requested a complete response by September 3, 2026, citing the proximity of the midterm elections and the scale of DOJ’s planned deployment.
title: Krishnamoorthi Demands Answers from Trump DOJ Over Reported Hiring of Lawyer Convicted of Hacking Election Websites for Election Monitoring

“The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect. Donald Trump can sign all the executive orders he wants, but it will always be Lake Ontario. Canada is not our enemy. When he is done doing arts and crafts in the Oval, I’d suggest he turn his attention to his failed economy that is raising costs, eliminating jobs, and leaving working men and women behind.”

Birmingham, AL - Today, U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell (AL-07) celebrated the Food and Drug Administration's approval of daraxonrasib, a new drug for treating advanced pancreatic cancer. This drug, taken as two pills a day, is the first treatment that substantially extends the lives of patients with pancreatic cancer.

"This is incredible news," celebrated Rep. Sewell. "No family in America has been spared the scourge of cancer, including my own. Having lost my mother, the late Nancy Gardner Sewell, to pancreatic cancer, I know firsthand the heartbreak and devastation this disease can bring to a family. That is why I am overjoyed to join millions of Americans in celebrating this historic victory which will help revolutionize the way we treat pancreatic cancer."

"The FDA’s approval of daraxonrasib offers new hope to pancreatic cancer patients and their loved ones, and represents a remarkable step forward in our fight against one of the deadliest forms of cancer," continued Rep. Sewell. "Breakthroughs like this one highlight why we must continue investing in lifesaving research - so that one day we will not only be able to treat pancreatic cancer, but cure it!”

Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest major cancers, with a five-year survival rate below 20%. This cutting-edge drug, which will be sold under the brand name Rasonque, was approved for patients who have metastatic pancreatic cancer and have already tried chemotherapy. In clinical trials, participants who received daraxonrasib lived for a median of over 13 months, compared with less than seven months for those who received chemotherapy. Some patients who have gotten the drug through clinical trials have lived for years.

This new breakthrough comes just months after the passage of the Nancy Gardner Sewell Multi-Cancer Early Detection Act, a bipartisan law that ensures seniors on Medicare can get access to the latest lifesaving cancer screening tests. Co-sponsored by Rep. Terri Sewell (D-AL) and Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), the bill was one of the most sponsored bill in the 199th Congress with 339 House co-sponsors and 68 Senate co-sponsors and was signed into law by President Trump on February 3, 2026.

###
title: Rep. Sewell Celebrates the FDA Approval of a New Drug for Pancreatic Cancer

DOVER, Del. — Today, U.S. Representative Sarah McBride and Lt. Governor Kyle Evans Gay (both D-Del.) brought together advocates, childcare providers, and local leaders for a conversation at Delaware State University on lowering childcare costs, expanding access to care, and strengthening Delaware’s childcare workforce.

Rep. McBride was recently selected by House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries to co-lead the House Democratic Caregiving Working Group, which is charged with helping develop the House Democratic Caucus’s legislative agenda on caregiving. Today’s discussion further informs that work, bringing the experiences and priorities of Delaware families and childcare providers directly into creating bold federal solutions to caregiving challenges facing families in the First State and across the country.

“Childcare costs are increasingly unaffordable for working families in Delaware and across the country,” said Rep. McBride. “Access to affordable, reliable childcare must be at the center of our economic agenda at both the federal and state levels. Today’s conversation brought together providers, advocates, and local leaders to talk about what it will take to lower costs for families, expand access to care, and recruit and retain the childcare workers our communities need. As we develop a caregiving agenda for the next Congress, I’m going to make sure the voices and experiences of Delawareans are front and center.”

The discussion focused on four key challenges facing Delaware families and childcare providers: affordability for families; access to and availability of care; financial, operational, and workforce pressures facing providers; as well as state and federal policies that could help address those challenges. Participants also discussed gaps in infant care, care during nontraditional hours, rural childcare, and care for children with disabilities, as well as barriers providers face in recruiting and retaining workers and expanding capacity to meet demand.

“For too long, we have approached early childhood education in Delaware as a collection of individual programs — each with its own funding stream, requirements, eligibility rules, and priorities. But parents don't experience government that way. Educators don’t. And children certainly don’t,” said Lt. Governor Kyle Evans Gay. “We have an opportunity right now to think differently — to move from fragmented programs toward an aligned and coordinated system with sustainable investments. We have the opportunity to design a system around the people that we serve. As Chair of the IRMC, I am committed to that work—and to making sure the we have the honest conversations about governance, financing, coordination, and accountability that this moment requires so that our youngest Delawareans have access to the education and care they need.”

Affordability was a central focus throughout the conversation as families continue to face high childcare costs. According to a recent report, the national average annual price of center-based infant care was $15,570. In Delaware, families are paying approximately $17,252 per year for center-based infant care.

Joining Rep. McBride and Lt. Governor Gay were representatives from:

Child Care for Every Family Network

Delaware Association for the Education of Young Children

YMCA of Delaware

Delaware State Education Association

Delaware State University's Early Childhood Center

Delaware Department of Education

Delaware Department of Health and Social Services

Representatives shared concerns about workforce infrastructure and the increasing costs of providing care, as well as squeezed bottom lines across the board. Each spoke about challenges facing the affordability of childcare — reinforcing the broad effects across every aspect of the economy and workforce — and shared invaluable perspectives about the way families are navigating childcare access and costs across Delaware.

Rep. McBride has long worked to strengthen support for working families. In Congress, she is a cosponsor of the Child Care for Every Community Act, which would create a universal childcare program, and the American Family Act, which would increase the value of a monthly Child Tax Credit.

While serving as a Delaware State Senator, Rep. McBride passed the Healthy Delaware Families Act with bipartisan support, providing paid family and medical leave to workers across the state. In Congress, she has continued to lead on strengthening the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and expanding paid leave nationwide. She has introduced legislation including the FAIR Leave Act, the Flexible Leave Act, and is an original cosponsor of the FAMILY Act, helping ensure workers and their families can access leave when they need it most.

Photos from the event can be found here.

Washington, DC – Yesterday, Congressman Gabe Amo (D-RI), Congressman James Walkinshaw (D-VA), Congresswoman Robin Kelly (D-IL), and Senator Edward J. Markey (D-MA) led 134 Members of Congress in demanding the Trump administration release international affairs funding, including Global Health Programs funding, before its expiration and stop proposed changes to the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR).

The unspent $7.5 billion in international affairs funding, including more than $3 billion for Global Health Programs, is set to expire on September 30, 2026. These funds provide most U.S. foreign health assistance, including funding to treat and prevent HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, and malnutrition. The Office of Management and Budget plans to use some of these funds to cover closeout costs for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), which would contradict congressional intent and lead to preventable deaths.

Additionally, the State Department’s proposed changes to PEPFAR will reduce the ability to provide HIV treatment and prevention, increasing the risk of the spread of HIV while hindering the Centers for Disease Control's ability to conduct disease surveillance and respond to outbreaks.

The Members write:

We write to express our alarm that approximately $7.5 billion in international affairs funding remains unobligated and at risk of expiring on September 30, 2026, including more than $3 billion of global health funding. These funds were enacted into law for specific purposes that support life-saving assistance, strengthen partners against shared threats, and reinforce American leadership, and the Administration has a legal obligation to execute such appropriations consistent with the law.

The Department and OMB’s refusal to spend GHP funding as directed by Congress and the concerning PEPFAR implementation changes defy the law and threaten lives—internationally and in the U.S.

“Last year, the Administration's disruption of PEPFAR programs resulted in 2 million fewer patients receiving lifesaving treatment, including 77,000 children,” said Dr. Sheila Davis, Chief Executive Officer at Partners In Health. “The closure of over 1,700 clinics and staffing cuts have also contributed to a tragic increase in mother-to-child transmission of HIV, which we know how to prevent. Today, the State Department and Office of Management and Budget continue to withhold funding and disrupt critical programs addressing HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, and other urgent health priorities. These funds were appropriated by Congress and signed into law by the President on a bipartisan basis. It is simply wrong to leave billions of dollars in duly approved funding unspent while patients around the world suffer the consequences. Partners In Health stands in solidarity with the patients and communities bearing the brunt of these policies. We are grateful to the members of Congress conducting oversight through this letter and other efforts to ensure these funds are released and lifesaving programs can continue.”

The full letter can be found here.

Gottheimer regularly visits small businesses across New Jersey’s Fifth District as part of his Josh on the Job series to hear directly from workers, owners, and customers about the issues impacting their jobs and their communities.

DES PLAINES, IL — Today, Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi joined local leaders from Des Plaines, Elk Grove Village, DuPage County, Bartlett, and Schaumburg to announce nearly $5.8 million in Community Project Funding he secured for five infrastructure projects across the 8th Congressional District. The investments will upgrade aging water infrastructure, reduce neighborhood flooding, improve road and pedestrian safety, and advance major transportation improvements.

“When a water main breaks, a neighborhood floods, or an intersection becomes overwhelmed, families pay the price,” said Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi. “That’s why I’m proud to have secured nearly $5.8 million to help our communities fix aging infrastructure before problems become crises. These investments will protect homes from flooding, keep drinking water reliable, and make our roads and intersections safer. With severe weather putting more strain on the infrastructure we rely on every day, investing now will help keep our communities safer, stronger, and more resilient for years to come.”

The funding includes:

$1.8 million for the City of Des Plaines’ Algonquin Road Grade Separation Project to support Phase II engineering, including final design and preparation of the plans and specifications needed to move the project toward construction. Phase II engineering is expected to take approximately three to four years.

$1.092 million for Elk Grove Village’s Water Main Lining Project to rehabilitate 15 critical sections of the Village’s more than 180 miles of water main, much of which dates to the 1950s and 1960s. The project will be Elk Grove Village’s first use of water-main lining, which requires less roadway excavation than traditional replacement.

$240,000 for DuPage County’s Newton & Second Flood Reduction Project to address recurring flooding in the Nelsons Highview neighborhood near Newton Avenue and Second Street in unincorporated Glendale Heights. Flooding has damaged residential properties and closed roads, limiting emergency vehicle access. Improvements include a detention/retention pond, additional storm sewers, and outlet and downstream improvements.

$1.5 million for the Village of Bartlett’s Route 25/West Bartlett Road Intersection Improvements to add dedicated turn lanes in each direction and a pedestrian crossing bridge to improve traffic flow and safety.

$1.152 million for the Village of Schaumburg’s Hammond Drive/Algonquin Road Intersection Improvements to improve the intersection and mitigate the impacts of industrial traffic on Schaumburg residents.

The five awards total $5.784 million in Fiscal Year 2026 Community Project Funding secured by Congressman Krishnamoorthi for infrastructure projects across the 8th Congressional District.
title: Krishnamoorthi Delivers Nearly $5.8 Million to Upgrade Aging Infrastructure, Protect Communities from Severe Weather Threats

Fredericksburg, Va. — On Monday, August 24, immediately following a roundtable with veterans in the community, Congressman Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) and Senator Tim Kaine (D-Va.) met with key leaders at the Fredericksburg VA Health Care Center (HCC). This meeting was a direct response to Vindman’s repeated calls for action to reduce wait times and improve care at this state-of-the-art facility.

After the productive meeting at the HCC, Vindman released the below statement.

“This week’s meeting with leadership at the Fredericksburg VA Health Care Center was productive and laid the groundwork for continued collaboration between the Department of Veterans Affairs and my office.

“I shared what I heard directly from local veterans at a roundtable earlier that day about staffing, access to care, and communication, and we discussed concrete steps the VA and my office can take together to address these challenges.

“I appreciate VA leadership coming to the table and acknowledging that too many veterans are still facing unreasonable wait times and delays. I feel confident that we will keep fighting, together, to make sure this facility is fully equipped to serve every veteran who depends on it. My office will continue to share updates on the tangible steps we take as a result of yesterday’s conversations.”

BACKGROUND

On Monday, August 24, Vindman hosted a roundtable with veterans from the community to discuss their experiences with the Fredericksburg VA Health Care Center. The roundtable helped highlight veterans’ stories, renewing the call to increase transparency and accountability at the VA.

In mid-July 2026, over 200 Virginians responded to a survey from Vindman about the delays they experienced at the Fredericksburg VA Health Care Center. He personally called over 30 of these veterans to express his commitment to demanding better from the VA.

In June 2026, Vindman introduced bipartisan legislation to increase transparency and accountability at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), helping address understaffing at facilities across the country, including the Fredericksburg VA Health Care Center, and ensure veterans receive the care they earned.

Prior to that, Vindman called for accountability and a clear timeline to bring the facility to full capacity, ensuring our nation’s veterans receive the care they earned through their service in six different letters.

Vindman sent the first letter to Secretary Collins raising the concern on staffing, wait times, and the ability to best serve veterans on April 10, 2025. Read the letter here.

Vindman sent the second letter to Secretary Collins raising the concern on staffing, wait times, and the ability to best serve veterans on October 6, 2025. Read the letter here.

Vindman sent the third letter to Secretary Collins raising the concern on staffing, wait times, and the ability to best serve veterans on October 17, 2025. Read the letter here.

Vindman sent the fourth letter to Secretary Collins raising the concern on staffing, wait times, and the ability to best serve veterans on October 27, 2025. Read the letterhere.

Vindman sent the fifth letter to Secretary Collins raising the concern on staffing, wait times, and the ability to best serve veterans on April 10, 2026. Read the letter here.

Vindman sent the sixth letter to Secretary Collins requesting an in-person meeting with the Health Care Center leadership on July 30, 2026. Read the letter here.
title: Vindman Meets with Leaders from Fredericksburg Health Care Center, Productive Discussion on How to Decrease Wait Times

Legislation Would Reauthorize Federal Grant Funding for Stormwater Infrastructure and Establish New Center of Excellence for the Great Lakes

BUFFALO, N.Y. – Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26), alongside Representatives Debbie Dingell (MI-06) and Nick Langworthy (NY-23), introduced the bipartisan Stormwater Treatment, Optimization, Resilience, and Management with Academic Technological Expertise and Research (STORMWATER) Act, legislation to strengthen communities’ ability to manage stormwater, reduce flooding, and protect local waterways from pollution. This legislation is endorsed by the Great Lakes Commission.

“Every Western New Yorker deserves to know that when the next major storm comes, our communities have the infrastructure and expertise to withstand it,” said Congressman Kennedy. “The STORMWATER Act is about making that investment now – strengthening our water infrastructure, protecting our neighborhoods and businesses, and putting Great Lakes communities at the forefront of the technologies we need to safeguard the critical waters we all call home.”

“It is crucial we have protective measures in place for overflows in our lakes. Michiganders know all too well how drastic weather conditions can cause millions of dollars in damages and risk people’s lives. This reauthorization will not only continue to fund these lifesaving agencies, but will establish a new facility in the Great Lakes Basin,” said Congresswoman Dingell.

“Communities across the Great Lakes region know firsthand the challenges that stormwater runoff and flooding can create for our homes, businesses, farms, and infrastructure,” said Congressman Langworthy. “The STORMWATER Act will strengthen research and innovation, support communities working to address flooding, and establish a dedicated Center of Excellence focused on the unique needs of the Great Lakes Basin. As a member of the Great Lakes Caucus, I’m proud to join Congressman Kennedy in advancing this legislation and ensuring our region has the tools and expertise needed to protect our communities and keep our Great Lakes healthy for generations to come.”

"The Great Lakes Commission commends Rep. Kennedy for introducing the STORMWATER Act, which will ensure the Stormwater Centers of Excellence program continues nationwide while recognizing the Great Lakes as a unique resource increasingly threatened by stormwater impacts,” said Tim Bruno, Chair of the Great Lakes Commission. “Communities across the Great Lakes region are confronting more frequent flooding that threatens public health and water quality, carrying nutrients, debris, chemicals and other pollutants into our waterways. This bill will provide crucial resources to help communities prepare for and address these growing challenges."

The STORMWATER Act would reauthorize federal grant programs established through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law that support stormwater innovation, technical assistance, and flood mitigation. The existing grant programs are currently set to expire in September 2026. The legislation would extend them through fiscal year 2031, providing communities with the resources and continuity needed to plan and implement long-term infrastructure improvements.

Critically for Western New York, the legislation would establish a Stormwater Center of Excellence specifically focused on the Great Lakes region. While four existing Stormwater Centers of Excellence currently provide regional expertise on stormwater infrastructure, there is no federally designated center focused specifically on the Great Lakes basin, a region containing approximately 21 percent of the world’s fresh water and 84 percent of North America’s surface fresh water. This Great Lakes-focused Center would ensure that communities across the region can access technical expertise tailored to their unique stormwater and water-quality challenges, including strategies to improve infrastructure, reduce flooding, and protect the lakes and waterways that are central to the region’s economy and quality of life.

Specifically, the STORMWATER Act would:

Establish a fifth Center of Excellence focused on the Great Lakes region, ensuring the region’s unique stormwater and water-quality challenges receive dedicated expertise;

Reauthorize $5 million annually from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 to support and maintain five Centers of Excellence;

Reauthorize $10 million annually from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for competitive Stormwater Control Infrastructure Project grants to support communities’ stormwater infrastructure needs.

Background

Stormwater runoff occurs when rain or melted snow cannot absorb into the ground and instead flows over hard surfaces like roads, rooftops, and parking lots. As that water moves rapidly into drainage systems and waterways, it can overwhelm infrastructure, contribute to flooding, and carry oil, debris, fertilizers, chemicals, and other pollutants into local streams and lakes.

For Western New York communities surrounded by the Great Lakes, these challenges are both environmental and economic. Stronger stormwater infrastructure can help protect homes and businesses from flooding, reduce pollution entering local waterways, and preserve the health and economic vitality of the Great Lakes for generations to come.

###
title: Kennedy Introduces Bipartisan STORMWATER Act to Strengthen Water Infrastructure and Protect Great Lakes Communities

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11), a member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs, Congressman Gabe Amo (RI-01), Congresswoman Robin Kelly (IL-02), and Senator Edward J. Markey (D-MA) led 134 of their colleagues in calling on Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought to immediately release $7.5 billion in international affairs funding, to include more than $3 billion in congressionally appropriated global health funding before it expires on September 30, 2026.

In a bicameral letter to Rubio and Vought, the lawmakers warned that approximately $7.5 billion in international affairs funding remains unobligated and at risk of expiring, including more than $3 billion intended for lifesaving global health programs.

The Global Health Programs account supports efforts to combat HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, malnutrition, and emerging health threats. According to the letter, OMB has notified Congress that approximately $1.35 billion is being withheld for costs associated with closing the U.S. Agency for International Development instead of being used for the critical global health programs Congress funded.

The lawmakers warned that allowing the funding to expire could contribute to an estimated 121,000 deaths from tuberculosis, 47,600 deaths from malaria, and the loss of lifesaving nutrition products for 22.9 million children.

“This hardship can be prevented if the Administration spends these funds as Congress directed,” the lawmakers wrote. “We call on you to immediately release the remaining lifesaving, bipartisan GHP funding before it expires on September 30, 2026.”

The letter also raises concerns about proposed changes to the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, which has saved more than 26 million lives. The lawmakers warned that reducing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s role in the program could disrupt HIV treatment, weaken global disease surveillance, and limit America’s ability to stop outbreaks abroad before they threaten communities at home.

“The Department and OMB’s refusal to spend GHP funding as directed by Congress and the concerning PEPFAR implementation changes defy the law and threaten lives, internationally and in the U.S.,” the lawmakers wrote.

Walkinshaw, Amo, Kelly, Markey, and their colleagues demanded answers by September 9 regarding the Administration’s plans to release the funding, the costs of terminating USAID programs, and the public-health consequences of reducing the CDC’s role in PEPFAR.

The full text of the letter, including the complete list of 138 signers, is available here.

###
title: Walkinshaw, Amo, Kelly, Markey Lead 134 Colleagues in Demanding Release of More Than $3 Billion in Lifesaving Global Health Funding
