PROVIDENCE, RI — Today, U.S. Representatives Seth Magaziner (RI-02) and Gabe Amo (RI-01) announced $2.9 million of funding awarded by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to the Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth and Families to improve mental health outcomes forchildren and youth with, or at risk of, serious emotional disturbances (SED).

“No one should have to struggle alone to get their child the mental health care they need,” said Magaziner. “This funding will strengthen access to care in Rhode Island so that kids facing serious emotional challenges can get the support they need early and have the opportunity to live happy, successful lives into adulthood.”

“Children struggling with their mental health and their families need our support,” said Amo. “This federal funding will help our dedicated mental health professionals support children and youth with severe emotional needs. Every struggling child deserves appropriate care so they can heal, grow, and thrive.”

The funding supports the Comprehensive Community Mental Health Services for Children and their Families Program, also known as the Children's Mental Health Initiative (CMHI), which provides resources to improve mental health outcomes for children and youth from birth through age 21 who are at risk for or living with serious emotional disturbances. Serious emotional disturbances, or SED, refer to mental, behavioral, or emotional conditions in children and youth that severely limit their ability to function at home or in school.

These include conditions such as severe anxiety, depression, trauma-related disorders, and other conditions that significantly disrupt a young person's daily life and development.

The program helps create the sustainable infrastructure and services designed to help children and youth with SED successfully transition into adulthood.

The funding, administered by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), supports services like in-home and community-based therapy, care coordination between schools, doctors, and social services, crisis intervention support, family and youth peer support programs, and case management to help families navigate the mental health system.
title: Magaziner, Amo Announce $2.9 Million for Mental Health Services for Children

text:
Washington D.C. – In an exclusive cover story for The Advocate, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi reflected on nearly four decades of advocacy alongside the LGBTQ community, from confronting the HIV/AIDS crisis and advancing landmark civil rights protections to the ongoing fight for transgender Americans.

As she prepares to conclude her historic tenure in Congress, Pelosi discussed the grassroots activism that powered decades of progress, her belief in the dignity and worth of every person and the work still ahead to defend LGBTQ rights and our Democracy.

Read the full story below:

The Advocate: Nancy Pelosi on AIDS, trans rights, the legacy she resists claiming — and why Democrats must ‘win big’

[By Christopher Wiggins, 8/18/26]

Tourists are already taking photographs outside Nancy Pelosi’s office when I arrive at the Longworth House Office Building at 10:30 on a Thursday morning with photographer Mike Nelson.

Inside, a staff member conducting a Zoom job interview asks an applicant, “Why are you interested in working in this office specifically?”

A framed display shows the men who had served as speaker of the House before Pelosi, their portraits arranged around the woman who broke the sequence.

“Speaker Pelosi, Christopher Wiggins with The Advocate is here to see you,” communications director Ian Krager says as he invites us inside her spacious office with a view of the Capitol dome.

Pelosi would speak with me for more than an hour, and would then keep talking through the photo session. She dislikes having her picture taken but had agreed to sit for a portrait.

Before my first question, Pelosi describes the tributes accompanying her final year in Congress. That morning, she had told Krager she wanted to discuss the future. But there is no talking to Pelosi about the future without touching on the recent past, if only so she can redistribute the credit. She announced in November that she would retire after nearly four decades in the House and two separate stints as speaker.

“I’ve got so many accolades, I’m embarrassed by it,” she confesses.

A month earlier, I had watched her at the Equality PAC National Pride Gala as a tribute video to her allyship played. Pelosi stood facing the screen, absorbed.

“Yes, I am,” she says when asked whether she is allowing herself a victory lap. “As long as it shows collaboration,” and “the courage of the members, the activism of outside groups,” she adds.

“It’s fun to see,” she admits. “But it is kind of embarrassing. Like, come on, all right, enough.”

Pelosi has spent her career in superlatives: the first woman speaker and one of her generation’s most effective legislative tacticians. Her job, as she sees it, is to make the government machinery answer the movement’s demand.

That understanding was forged in death.

“BECAUSE I DID”

Pelosi entered Congress in June 1987 after winning a special election to succeed Democratic Rep. Sala Burton, a San Francisco organizer who took office after the 1983 death of her husband, the liberal power broker Phillip Burton. The widow-turned-congresswoman died of colon cancer on February 1, 1987, but not before urging Pelosi to seek the seat.

Pelosi, then 47, faced Harry Britt, a gay former San Francisco supervisor and Harvey Milk ally, in a fierce runoff during the AIDS catastrophe. She won on June 2.

One week later, in her first House floor speech, she said she had come to Congress to fight AIDS.

“Why’d you say you came here to fight AIDS?” Pelosi recalled people asking.

“Because I did,” she answered.

Pelosi, now 86, speaks of those years not as distant policy history, but as an emergency she can still enter at will. People were dying. Activists were accused of being too aggressive.

“Too aggressive when people are dying?” she asks, her voice sharpening.

“When we talk about HIV/AIDS, this was a matter of life and death,” Pelosi says. “I saw my role as one that could say to people: ‘You’re wrong. This is appropriate.’”

The AIDS movement became a model. People learned they could not wait quietly for institutions to notice them. They had to organize and make inaction politically impossible.

Conceived by activist Cleve Jones, the AIDS Memorial Quilt transformed an epidemic into individual lives rendered in fabric, photographs, lettering, and love.

However, Pelosi initially doubted Jones’s vision.

“Who sews anymore?” she remembers thinking. People did. They sewed by the thousands.

Once the quilt came alive, Pelosi fought to place the full display on the National Mall. The National Park Service had proposed only a few panels along a street.

“They didn’t know,” she says, smiling.

“Don’t mess with Nancy Pelosi,” I offer.

“The grassroots,” she corrects gently.

Pelosi also recalls the effort to bring the 1984 Democratic National Convention to San Francisco, when competing cities exploited fears of gay people and the emerging epidemic. Some warned that delegates could not safely eat the city’s food.

When members from the DNC site selection committee visited, Pelosi hosted them alongside representatives from the city’s Black, Asian, Latino, and gay and lesbian communities at her home. She instructed her children to make antigay prejudice visible — then disarm it.

“On the table, there’ll be the guacamole and the dip and all this stuff,” she recalls telling them. “When these people come up to the table, make sure — and I did myself — that you have a gay person right with you and both of you dip into the stuff at the same time.”

This act challenged fears that AIDS spread through shared food or casual contact. Pelosi also remembered physicians touching patients without gloves in front of reporters, turning human contact into an intervention against panic.

Pelosi helped secure billions of dollars of federal support for research, treatment, housing, and prevention. “We’re not talking about money,” she says. “We’re talking about saving lives.” She remembers monthly meetings in which people with AIDS initially asked for help making wills or finding medicine overseas. Then science advanced, and the requests changed.

THE RULES ARE YOUR PROTECTION

Pelosi’s reverence for mobilization is only matched by her institutional competence.

As chair of the California Democratic Party, she urged activists to attend meetings where rules were written — and to learn those rules before declaring themselves mistreated.

“You were out of order,” she remembers telling people who complained that a chair had ruled against them. “The rules are your best protection.”

In Congress, that meant understanding procedure and legislation’s full path. A triumphant floor amendment could disappear in conference. “Anticipation, anticipation, anticipation,” she says.

Pelosi distinguishes the power she once held from the influence she retains. Power, in her telling, is executive and urgent. A speaker must balance competing concerns and act within the available window.

“If you hesitate, you’ll lose your opportunities,” she says.

Influence is a suggestion, a “gentler touch,” wisdom exercised by someone who no longer controls the votes or calendar.

“I have given up power,” Pelosi says, “but I have not given up influence.”

As if to illustrate the point, her cellphone rings. Rahm Emanuel — the former congressman, Obama White House chief of staff, Chicago mayor, and U.S. ambassador to Japan — was calling. Pelosi chuckles and hands the phone to Krager, who silences it. Later, it rings again, though I could not see the caller. Even without the gavel, the political world still has Nancy Pelosi on speed dial.

Her mentorship follows a simple principle. She asks younger people to identify their “why,” devise a strategy, and show why the objective serves others.

“It has to be their thing,” she says. “What is your passion? What is your mission?”

That philosophy will shape the Nancy Pelosi Institute for Representative Democracy at the University of California, Berkeley, scheduled to launch in January. Pelosi is expected to help teach a course there on Congress.

“THEY PICK TRANS”

Pelosi’s LGBTQ+ record includes the passage of the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, the rescinding of a ban on gay people serving openly in the military through the Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell Repeal Act of 2010, the federal recognition of same-sex marriage through the Respect for Marriage Act, and the repeated House passage of the Equality Act.

She uses those victories to explain the right’s fixation on transgender people.

“They know that there’s no argument about LGBT,” she says. “So they pick trans.”

Decades of organizing, she argues, made broad attacks on gay and lesbian people less useful. Republicans identified transgender people — and bathrooms, sports, and military service — as terrain where unfamiliarity could become fear.

“They lost the battle on HIV/AIDS, on anti-discrimination and everything,” Pelosi says. “Now what they’re doing to the military is harmful to our national security.”

Since returning to office, the Trump administration has sought to exclude transgender people from military service, restricted passport gender markers, and targeted federal support for gender-affirming care.

“It’s heartbreaking,” Pelosi says. “These are people’s children.”

She has a transgender grandniece whom she loves dearly. She has met homeless transgender youth rejected by their relatives, and families who embraced their children “and took pride” in them.

“That’s where we want everyone to be,” she says. Pelosi rejects the idea that San Francisco is merely tolerant.

“That’s a condescending word,” she says as she often does. “We have respect, and we take pride.”

In 2019, during Trump’s first attempt to restrict transgender military service, Pelosi invited transgender Army officers Jennifer Peace and Ian Brown to the State of the Union. When I call them her guests, she corrects me.

“They’re my friends,” she says.

The current policy is a bitter reversal after “don’t ask, don’t tell” — another demand that some people serve by concealing themselves. Pelosi sees unfinished work as proof that progress creates new expectations.

“The successes have bred more challenges,” she says.

“I’M NOT AN INCREMENTALIST”

Pelosi bristles when I ask what she had learned about incrementalism.

“I’m not an incrementalist,” she says. “It’s just not my thing.”

The assertion collides with a defining dispute. In 2007, Pelosi supported an Employment Non-Discrimination Act protecting sexual orientation but not gender identity. It passed the House but died in the Senate. Many transgender people remember the exclusion as a betrayal.

When pressed, she points to her approach to passing the Hate Crimes Prevention Act just two years later. During that fight, she says, members warned that the bill could not advance with gender identity protections intact.

“They came back to me and said, ‘We can’t get it out of committee with trans in there,’” Pelosi recalls. “‘But you could pass it in a minute if you take out trans.’”

Her answer, she says, was categorical. “We won’t pass it in a hundred years if we take out trans,” she remembers saying. “We’re never bringing that bill to the floor. It’s all-inclusive.”

The legislation remained inclusive and became law in 2009. Judy Shepard came to Washington to lobby for it, accompanied, Pelosi recalls, by the sheriff from the Wyoming county where her son, Matthew, was murdered. He told lawmakers he might once have opposed them but had “seen the light.”

The following year, Congress repealed “don’t ask, don’t tell.” Pelosi remembers promising at a Harvey Milk commemoration that the work would be finished by Christmas. President Barack Obama signed the repeal on December 22, 2010.

In 2022, Congress passed the Respect for Marriage Act, requiring federal and interstate recognition of valid same-sex and interracial marriages. It became the final enrolled bill Pelosi signed as speaker.

When I ask whether she ever sits alone and thinks, Damn, look at what I’ve done,Pelosi permits herself a moment.

“I may soon do that,” she says with a smile.

A SPARK OF DIVINITY

When I ask what she hopes the LGBTQ+ community would remember about her, Pelosi resists the premise.

“I don’t really think it’s about me,” she says.

I ask her to indulge me. “I would be glad it is not the opposite — that I stood in the way of anything,” she says. “Because of everything we did, I would want the story to be that I was part of something. That it was a collaboration, a wedding of inside maneuvering, outside mobilization, and respect.”

Then she remembers an awards ceremony honoring Jones, who had opposed her in her first congressional campaign before becoming a close friend. The activist told the audience that in 100 years, nobody would remember the people in the room or what they had done — with one exception.

He turned and bowed toward Pelosi.

“Oh my God,” she recalls thinking. “Why did he do that?”

It brought her to tears.

Pelosi wants history to remember a movement, while history insists on assigning a face. Accepting her place in it seems perilously close to diminishing everyone else’s.

Pelosi describes herself as a devout Catholic. San Francisco Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone directed priests in 2022 not to admit her to communion because she supported abortion rights. The archdiocese said the action was not excommunication, though Pelosi uses that word colloquially in our conversation.

“That’s the archbishop’s problem, not mine,” she says.

Her faith begins with the belief that every person carries a “spark of divinity.” Christ’s participation in humanity, she says, lets people participate in the divine. Dignity cannot depend on nationality, housing status, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

“How can they not believe that if they have the spark of divinity, so does everybody else, no matter how different we may be?” she asks.

Pelosi, who takes issue with “un-Christian Christians,” searches for a description of religious figures who claim faith while excluding whole categories of people.

“Partners in inhumanity,” she says.

“All God’s children,” she adds, describing their apparent creed, “except we’ll decide who.”

She connects the idea to civil rights icon John Lewis, whose moral authority ended a caucus dispute over adding LGBTQ+ protections to the Civil Rights Act via the Equality Act.

“John Lewis just said, ‘This is what we’re doing,’” Pelosi recalls. That ended the discussion.

“A MOBILIZATION OF LOVE”

Pelosi is leaving Congress amid a second Trump administration she regards with disgust. She avoids saying the president’s name whenever possible, referring to him as “you know who.”

“Any time spent on him is just repulsive to me,” she says.

She accuses congressional Republicans of surrendering the legislative branch’s independence. “They have surrendered Article One,” Pelosi says.

She lists what she believes is under strain: free and fair elections, an independent judiciary, the rule of law, due process, and freedom of the press.

“All of these things chilled, if not destroyed,” she says, then retreats slightly. “Chilled.”

Pelosi predicts Democrats will win the House in November and hopes they will capture the Senate. But she returns to the source of political change: public sentiment awakened by personal connection.

People are busy with work and family, she says. Movements must pierce that noise and make the stakes legible.

She remembers people who questioned her AIDS work changing when someone in their family became sick or came out. “It was a mobilization of love too,” she says.

Movements, in Pelosi’s telling, turn the person labeled “other” into someone already loved. They make abstraction impossible. The same process, she believes, will undermine anti-transgender attacks.

Near the end of our conversation, Pelosi distills the legacy she has spent nearly the entire interview trying not to claim.

“If I’m remembered,” she says, she hopes HIV and AIDS advocacy would be “one of the main reasons.”

Her service, she says, was grounded in “respect for the dignity and worth of every person.” And that she was “especially honored to be associated with the LGBTQ community.”

Then come the photographs.

She says she has disliked taking pictures since childhood when her father was the mayor of Baltimore. Nelson coaxes her toward the window.

“They usually say to me, ‘Don’t smile,’” she tells him. “That’s impossible.”

Even during the photo session, she returns to the next generation. The victories of her era, Pelosi says, should already be “in the dustbin of history” — settled questions rather than recurring emergencies. Instead, transgender people remain targets.

Nelson asks her to look toward the window, where the early-afternoon light falls across the former speaker, who has spent a career recognizing openings.

The camera clicks.

As the office resumes its schedule, Pelosi prepares to travel again. New York. Missouri. Chicago. More politics. The midterm elections loom.

And the woman at the center of the frame — the one surrounded in the reception room by all the men who came before her — is still thinking about what comes next.

“We have to win,” she says. “We have to win big.”
title: ICYMI: Pelosi Reflects On Historic LGBTQ Progress And The Fight Ahead In Exclusive Interview With The Advocate

Stanton Celebrates Four Years of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Alongside Arizona Retirees
TEMPE – U.S. Representative Greg Stanton (AZ-04) joined retirees and community advocates from the Arizona Alliance for Retired Americans (AARA) for a roundtable marking four years since the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The discussion focused on how the landmark law has lowered prescription drug costs and solutions to healthcare expenses that continue to strain seniors’ budgets.
“Four years ago, I took on Big Pharma and fought to get legislation signed into law that would finally empower Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices for seniors. Today I proudly celebrate the progress we’ve made, alongside advocates like the AARA,” said Rep. Stanton. “I’ll keep fighting in Congress to expand these savings, strengthen Medicare, and make sure Arizonans can retire with dignity.”
Stanton strongly supported the Inflation Reduction Act, which made major changes to Medicare Part D and Part B to lower drug costs. The law established a $2,000 out-of-pocket cap, capped insulin costs at $35 per month, made recommended vaccines available at no cost for people with Medicare Part D, expanded low-income subsidies, and empowered Medicare to negotiate drug prices.
In Arizona’s Fourth Congressional District alone, approximately 26,000 Medicare beneficiaries saved a combined $6 million on their prescriptions in 2024 because of the law’s drug pricing provisions. AZ-04 Constituent Doug Hart, who has been on Medicare for 15 years, shared during the roundtable how the IRA has helped him save up to $5,000 a year in out-of-pocket drug costs.
“Prescription drug costs are one of the biggest financial pressures facing older Arizonans, and no senior should have to choose between filling a prescription and paying for groceries, housing, or utilities," said Linda Somo, President of the Arizona Alliance for Retired Americans. "The Inflation Reduction Act took historic steps to lower those costs by finally giving Medicare the power to negotiate lower prices with drug companies and by capping what people with Medicare have to pay out of pocket for their prescriptions. These protections are already making a real difference for retirees living on fixed incomes. We need to build on this progress and make prescription drugs more affordable for all of us."
During the event, Stanton also received a 2026 Retiree Hero Certificate for his 100% pro-retiree score, earned through his 2025 work to lower prescription drug costs and defend access to healthcare amid Republican efforts to scale back coverage.
title: Stanton Celebrates Four Years of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Alongside Arizona Retirees

PENN HILLS, PA – Today, Congressman Chris Deluzio (PA-17) was in Penn Hills, Pennsylvania to celebrate that he secured $850,000 in federal funding for the Verona Road Bridge Replacement in Penn Hills. At the check presentation and press conference, Congressman Deluzio was joined by State Representative Joe McAndrew, Penn Hills Mayor Pauline Calabrese, Jason Zang, District Executive for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's (PennDOT) Engineering District 11, and other Penn Hills and Verona leaders.

“I’m proud that I secured $850,000 in federal funding to help replace and upgrade the bridge on Verona Road in Penn Hills,” said Congressman Deluzio. “Our community should have the best infrastructure out there, and I’m proud I could help Penn Hills and PennDOT do this important bridge replacement. I’ll always fight to bring home federal money to make life better for all of us in Western Pennsylvania.”

The Verona Road Bridge Replacement project would replace the full existing bridge over Sandy Creek between Mt. Carmel Rd and Lincoln Rd. It would be replaced with a structure that would ensure the safety and reliability of this State Route 2058 corridor. The proposed project would improve any structural and geometric deficiencies of the existing bridge and approach roadway to ensure uninterrupted traffic movements and reduce ongoing maintenance costs. According to PennDOT, the full project cost is $4.7 million and is expected to complete construction at the end of 2028.

“We are seeing real injections of infrastructure project funding in our region because we want to maintain this infrastructure for generations to come. This project is a testament to the fact that we see an issue that is not just effecting the roadway, but also the primary source of funding for our Fire Department, Engine #221, and we are address this issue for the region.” – Pennsylvania State Representative Joe McAndrew (House District 32)

“We are grateful that Congressman Deluzio once again is delivering real results for us. His work to secure funding for this critical project directly protects public safety by clearing the way for emergency vehicles, school buses, and our residents who drive over that bridge every day.” – Pauline Calabrese, Mayor of Penn Hills

“Congressman Deluzio has been a strong advocate for transportation funding in Western Pennsylvania and consistently delivers critical funding year after year. We are extremely grateful for the funding secured for this critical link for the community. The Verona Road Bridge project, when complete, will continue to serve the community for many years to come.” – Jason Zang, District Executive for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's (PennDOT) Engineering District 11

This $850,000 PennDOT award is one of Congressman Deluzio’s community funding project selections for Fiscal Year (FY) 2026. He secured more than $193 million for fourteen projects across his Western Pennsylvania district, earning the title as the U.S. House Democrat who secured the most funding for their district out of the FY 2026 spending bills. He is third out of all U.S. House Members—of which there are 435. More details on all of those here.

Photos and video from the event are available here.

WASHINGTON — Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-08), a senior member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today led 13 of their Illinois colleagues in sending a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche calling on the Trump Administration to end its use of so-called “mega master” immigration hearings, mass proceedings in which as many as 185 noncitizens can be called to court on a single docket. The lawmakers warn that the Department of Justice (DOJ) is intentionally overcrowding dockets with little notice to immigrants in an effort to increase removal orders and advance the Trump Administration’s mass deportation campaign.

The other signers of the letter were U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and U.S. Representatives Danny Davis (D-IL-07), Jonathan Jackson (D-IL-01), Delia Ramirez (D-IL-03), Jesús G. “Chuy” García (D-IL-04), Nikki Budzinski (D-IL-13), Sean Casten (D-IL-06), Mike Quigley (D-IL-05), Eric Sorensen (D-IL-17), Bill Foster (D-IL-11), Jan Schakowsky (D-IL-09), Brad Schneider (D-IL-10), and Robin Kelly (D-IL-02).

In the letter, the lawmakers write:

“Through these hearings, the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) is intentionally overcrowding dockets with little notice to immigrants in an effort to manufacture significant numbers of removal orders and advance the Administration’s mass deportation campaign. Reports suggest that DOJ is calling as many as 185 noncitizens to court on a single docket, an action designed to drive mass deportations through chaos and confusion.”

In May, DOJ’s EOIR instituted a policy requiring judges in non-detained immigration courts to conduct master calendar hearings for 100 individuals twice per week while also maintaining their previously scheduled dockets and individual merits hearings. Many of those appearing have never been inside a courtroom, are unrepresented, do not speak English or Spanish fluently, do not understand the requirements of immigration proceedings, and are seeking asylum. In Chicago, the median notice time given to immigrants to appear in court fell from 229 days in May to just 34 days in June.

The lawmakers continue:

“Courtrooms handling upwards of 150 respondents in a judge’s morning docket raise serious concerns about whether individuals are receiving a meaningful opportunity to be heard. Dozens of unrepresented respondents appear in a single hearing, in courtrooms designed to accommodate approximately 25 individuals. This limits meaningful opportunities for them to understand their rights, seek legal representation, or even obtain adequate translations while in the hearing.”

The lawmakers also warn about mega master hearings involving children, particularly unaccompanied children who may have already experienced trauma, abuse, and exploitation and have limited access to legal counsel. These proceedings can make it harder for unaccompanied children to understand what is happening, ask questions, identify errors, or communicate with attorneys, advocates, or caregivers.

In Illinois, the letter places the mega master hearings alongside other elements of the Trump Administration’s mass deportation campaign, including Operation Midway Blitz, the attempted deployment of the National Guard in Chicago, and repeated attempts to withhold federal funding based on policy disagreements. The lawmakers argue that mega master hearings at the Chicago Immigration Court are the latest example of policies prioritizing enforcement and deportation quotas over due process while creating fear, confusion, and uncertainty for Illinois communities.

The members requested responses by September 1, 2026, including answers to the following questions:

In light of policy changes regarding preliminary asylum interviews, what procedures is DOJ using to ensure that each asylum applicant receives a full and fair evaluation of the merits of their claim?

What factors account for the significant reduction in hearing notice periods between May and June 2026 in immigration courts?

What steps are being taken to ensure respondents in immigration court receive adequate notice of their proceedings?

What is the appropriate process for a respondent in immigration court to request additional time to obtain an attorney?

What measures is DOJ taking to ensure that unrepresented respondents are afforded adequate due process, including having sufficient notice to appear before an immigration court?

How is the DOJ ensuring that the current immigration court system has adequate personnel, meets courtroom capacity needs, and provides staff with the proper administrative resources to manage these increased caseloads and to ensure due process for every noncitizen respondent?

In response to a question for the record from Senator Padilla after your Senate Judiciary Committee nomination hearing, you stated that all master calendar hearings are conducted “fully in accordance with the applicable law….” Please specify what applicable laws were referred to in this response.

In your response to Senator Padilla, you also stated that when individuals appearing at mega master hearings have “specific questions or concerns, immigration judges will hear those cases individually as appropriate.” What are the protocols or policies in place to ensure respondents appearing at mega master hearings be heard? How should a respondent request that a case be heard “individually”?

The lawmakers conclude:

“We urge the Administration to discontinue practices that undermine due process, including the use of mega master hearings. Instead, the Administration should ensure that asylum seekers receive fair and meaningful hearings and uphold the integrity of our nation’s immigration system.”
title: Krishnamoorthi, Durbin Lead Illinois Democratic Delegation in Calling on Trump Administration to End Mass Immigration Hearings Scheduling Up to 185 People at a Time

Lawmakers warn Dennis Kirk’s partisan record threatens the independence of Interior’s Inspector General as the office weighs at least four major corruption investigations

Washington, D.C. – Today, House Natural Resources Committee Democratic leaders sent a letter to Dennis Kirk, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Department of the Interior Office of the Inspector General, instructing him to preserve all federal records and demanding answers about potential document destruction inside the department that may have already happened.

The letter was signed by Ranking Member Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee Ranking Member Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.), Federal Lands Ranking Member Joe Neguse (D-Colo.), Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee Ranking Member Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), Water, Wildlife, and Fisheries Subcommittee Ranking Member Val Hoyle (D-Ore.), and Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee Ranking Member Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“Your nomination arrives at a time when the OIG has been asked to investigate multiple credible and well-evidenced allegations of corruption,” the lawmakers wrote. “But your heavily partisan record and lack of relevant experience raise questions about the potential impact of your tenure on the otherwise nonpartisan watchdog inside the Department of the Interior. Reports that officials at DOI have engaged in a pattern of records destruction increase the urgency of this matter.”

The lawmakers pointed to Kirk’s co-authorship of a chapter of Project 2025 and his record at the Intelligence Community Inspector General, where he appears to have served in a partisan role reporting to Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard during the office’s investigation into Signalgate. His nomination follows President Trump’s firing of over 21 inspectors general across the federal government shortly after taking office.

“An Inspector General whose loyalty to the President takes precedence over the mission of the offices of the inspectors general poses a threat to that independence,” the lawmakers wrote.

The letter lists at least four consequential investigations launched by Congressional Democrats the OIG is undertaking into high-ranking administration officials, including allegations of family favoritism and ethics violations against Dr. Jenifer Chatfield, a $3.5 million family windfall tied to a lithium mine approved with help from Karen Budd-Falen’s office, potential ethics violations by Bureau of Ocean Energy Management head Matt Giacona, and a Senate request to investigate what Interior officials knew about engineering failures at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The lawmakers also cited reporting that Interior officials have routinely shredded official documents and used disappearing Signal messages to avoid preserving communications as required by the Federal Records Act (FRA).

“Destruction of federal records implies there is something to hide,” the lawmakers wrote.

The letter closes, “Since arriving at the OIG, if you have engaged in document destruction of any kind, including shredding, the use of unauthorized messaging, automatic message deletion settings, or personal email for official business, this letter serves an instruction to stop. You are expected to maintain full compliance with the FRA.”

Read the full request to Dennis Kirk here.

###
title: Top Natural Resources Committee Democrats Question Independence of Trump’s Interior Watchdog Pick, Order Him to Preserve Records Amid Shredding Reports

(Rochester, N.Y.)—Today, Congressman Joe Morelle was joined by Rochester community health centers and advocates to announce the introduction of his Improving Health Through Integrated Food and Nutrition Services at Federally Qualified Health Centers Act, legislation he authored to help community health centers integrate food and nutrition services directly into patient care.

The announcement comes as FQHCs face increased pressure following the enactment of Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill, which makes deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP at a time when families are already struggling with the cost of food and healthcare.

“Access to healthy food and access to quality healthcare are deeply connected, and families should not have to navigate one system after another just to get the basic support they need,” said Congressman Joe Morelle. “At the same time President Trump and Congressional Republicans are cutting Medicaid and SNAP through their Big Ugly Bill, community health centers are being asked to do even more for the people who rely on them. My legislation gives these trusted local providers practical tools to meet patients where they are, connect them with nutritious food and existing assistance, and help people stay healthier in the first place.”

“At Trillium Health, we see every day how access to nutritious food directly affects a person's ability to stay healthy and manage chronic conditions,” said Jason Barnecut-Kearns, President and CEO of Trillium Health. “For example, patients with diabetes, heart disease, and hypertension cannot effectively manage their conditions without reliable access to nutritious food. Meanwhile, the need continues to grow. Trillium Health operates one of Rochester’s largest food pantries, and in 2026 alone, we have already provided food to over 2,800 households. Congressman Morelle's legislation recognizes what community health centers have long understood: access to nutritious food is fundamental to good health, and community health centers need sustainable resources to support this work. We are extremely grateful for Congressman Morelle's leadership and his commitment to improving health outcomes for the communities we serve.”

“Every day at Jordan Health, we see firsthand how access to nutritious food directly impacts a person's health and well-being. Too often, patients are forced to choose between paying for food, medication, housing, or other basic necessities," said Dr. Fredrick Johnson, Interim President and CEO of Jordan Health. "Congressman Morelle's legislation recognizes that healthcare extends beyond the walls of a medical exam room. This legislation would be critical for our Lifestyle Medicine Program, which is focused on nutrition and the development of healthy choices and improving health outcomes. We are grateful for Congressman Morelle's leadership and commitment to ensuring that Federally Qualified Health Centers have the tools necessary to care for the whole person.”

President and CEO of Oak Orchard Community Health Center Marco C. Altieri said, “Community health centers understand that good health is about more than what happens in the exam room. Access to healthy food can have a tremendous impact on a person’s ability to manage chronic conditions and live a healthier life. Congressman Morelle’s legislation recognizes that connection and gives FQHCs practical tools to better support the whole person. We are grateful for his continued leadership and his commitment to strengthening community health centers and the communities we serve.”

Dr. Mike Weston, Executive Director of His Branches, said: "Many of our patients continue to struggle with access to affordable and nutritious food. Those in this position continue to experience a reduced quality of health, lower life satisfaction, and shorter life expectancy. Congressman Morelle's proposal will create not only greater access for food, but also a greater collaboration between patients and clinicians in order to develop medically tailored strategies leading to stronger bodies and minds across our region."

Millions of Americans struggle to access enough healthy food, creating additional challenges for people managing chronic conditions like diabetes and heart disease. FQHCs are uniquely positioned to address that challenge because they already care for patients who are disproportionately affected by food insecurity, chronic disease, and limited access to affordable, nutritious food. Here in the Rochester region, community health centers are already working tirelessly to address these barriers, but there’s still more work to be done.

Congressman Morelle’s legislation would establish a competitive grant program through the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to give FQHCs additional resources to integrate food and nutrition support into care.

Specifically, the legislation would allow participating health centers to:

Screen patients for food insecurity during regular visits;

Operate on-site food pantries;

Partner with local food banks, farms, and nutrition assistance programs;

Hire registered dietitians and other nutrition professionals;

Provide culturally tailored nutrition education; and

Help streamline patient referrals and enrollment in programs including SNAP and WIC.

The legislation would also provide health centers with technical assistance to integrate these services into care delivery and support data collection and evaluation. It authorizes $100 million annually from FY27 through FY31 to support the grant program. By bringing those services together, Morelle’s legislation would help community health centers address a challenge they already see every day while giving patients a simpler path to the resources they need to stay healthy.

“I’m grateful to our community health centers for the extraordinary work they do every day,” Morelle continued. “I look forward to working with them and all of my colleagues to build support for this legislation in Congress and see it signed into law.”

LUMPKIN, G.A. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, along with Congressmembers Henry C. “Hank” Johnson, Jr. (GA-04), Nikema Williams (GA-05), Valerie Foushee (NC-04), and Deborah Ross (NC-02), today conducted oversight at the Stewart Detention Center.

“We are horrified by the situation here at Stewart,” said Jayapal. “We believe this detention center should be shut down. What we heard from detained people today was that they are not getting the care, the proper food, or the clean water that ICE says they are — to the point that we heard from several people who are simply not drinking water that they haven’t bought bottled from the commissary. Stewart is a failure of the promise of America, and I will continue working to get this facility, and all private, for-profit detention centers, shut down.”

“Stewart Detention Center has a long history of denying basic human dignity and rights to detainees. Since he took office, the Stephen Miller, Steve Bannon, bandwagon that has been rolling throughout the country collecting immigrants and then depositing them into facilities like Stewart Detention Facility, where they languish for months and even years at a time,” said Johnson.

“We conducted an oversight visit to Stewart Detention Center because accountability requires seeing firsthand how people in our nation’s immigration detention system are being treated. Some of the people detained in facilities like this came to this country with their parents at two or three years old—this is the only country they have ever called home. Yet they are being held as if they are hardened criminals. I will continue to do this work because everyone in this country, regardless of where they were born or their documentation status, deserves to be treated with dignity and respect,” said Williams.

“It was heart-wrenching to hear detained people talk about their stories and the family members that they have left. We heard from a gentleman whose wife has end stage renal disease, and she’s not getting the proper care. For people not to be able to have contact and have to constantly be worried about the conditions of their family members back home is another level of cruelty that has been added to the conditions under which they live. We didn’t get a whole lot of answers, but we saw a lot of things,” said Foushee.

“You cannot make money off the backs of immigrants and poor people. It is inhumane. It is unjust. And it is your taxpayer dollars, at least $150 a day to hold people who shouldn’t even be in detention in the first place. This has got to stop now,” said Ross.

Immigration advocates have criticized Stewart as one of the worst detention facilities in the country and many of its problems have persisted throughout Stewart’s history. Federal agencies, independent watchdogs, facility staff, detained people, and advocates have documented abuses including unsanitary conditions, inadequate and inedible food, medical neglect, poor mental health care, inappropriate and overuse of solitary confinement, and use of force.

Stewart has also been consistently overcrowded since Trump came into office. As of the week of July 27, the facility was over capacity by a few hundred. There have also been two suicides at the facility since Trump returned to office.

Members toured the facility and met with detained persons to hear about conditions directly from them. Their full takeaways can be found here.
title: Jayapal, Johnson, Williams, Foushee, Ross Conduct Oversight at Stewart Detention Center

Agawam, MA — On Tuesday, August 18, Congressman Richard E. Neal joined Agawam Mayor Chris Johnson, city councilors, and local officials to highlight the impact of federal investments made possible by the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). More than $1.5 billion has been invested across the First Congressional District.

In Agawam, $42.8 million was invested in projects and initiatives, with funding streams including:

$23.8 million in funding from the ARPA, consisting of $8.6 million in Coronavirus Local Fiscal Recovery funding and $15.2 million in Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief III funding.

$19 million in funding from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act

“Agawam is fortunate to have great leadership in Mayor Johnson and the City Council, who were able to identify three pressing challenges that otherwise may have gone unaddressed for several years. Enabling local governments to pursue critical investments that might otherwise remain out of reach is precisely what we intended, and I could not be more pleased to join with the Town in celebrating their achievements,” said Congressman Neal. “This tour is a reminder as to why our Founding Fathers entrusted the power of the purse with Congress: we understand the needs of our communities, and we have the responsibility to deliver the federal dollars needed to address them. The investments we are highlighting on this tour speak to that very notion, and I look forward to seeing the tangible results of our efforts.”

As a result of the ARPA, the Town of Agawam was able to complete three major infrastructure projects, including:

$3.8 million for the Meadow Street Drainage Improvements and Water Main Replacement Project. This project resolved chronic flooding issues and replaced approximately 7,100 linear feet of aging water main. The improvements have strengthened system resilience, enhanced water quality and pressure, and improved fire-flow protection.

$2.6 million for the North Westfield Street Culvert Replacement Project. This project replaced a deteriorating culvert that had previously required emergency intervention. The new structure improves roadway safety, protects key utility infrastructure, and ensures long-term reliability along a critical connection between Agawam and Westfield.

$1.9 million for the North Street Culvert Replacement Project. This project addressed a failing and undersized culvert, improving stormwater flow, reducing erosion, and bringing the crossing into compliance with current standards while protecting nearby utilities and environmental resources. This project was also supported by a $1.28 million earmark secured by Congressman Neal.

“Congressman Neal’s leadership has greatly benefited the Town of Agawam and its residents and businesses,” said Mayor Johnson. “The Town was able to complete over $8 million dollars of critical infrastructure projects with American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds, including the replacement of two major stormwater culverts. In addition, Congressman Neal was able to secure the necessary funding to replace a failing portion of a major sewer interceptor near the Westfield River. Finally, Congressman Neal’s support of the Inflation Reduction Act with its clean energy initiatives will likely result in the Town receiving substantial tax credit funding for its new high school which is served by a geothermal heating and cooling system.”

In addition to the ARPA, MassDOT has received $19 million from the IIJA and the IRA to support infrastructure projects that will benefit the Town of Agawam, including:

Pavement and bridge preservation on Route 57.

Improvements to Robinson Park Elementary School.

Guide and traffic sign replacement on I-291 and sections of Route 5.

The Town will also receive tax credits through the IRA for the new Agawam High School. These tax credits will help finance the school’s geothermal heating and cooling system.

August 17, 2026

WASHINGTON – Today, members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation, including U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks and Representatives Steny Hoyer, Glenn Ivey, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Sarah Elfreth, and Johnny Olszewski (all D-Md.), released the following statement regarding the State of Maryland’s victory in its lawsuit to restore the FBI headquarters project to Greenbelt, Maryland:

“For years, Team Maryland has fought to bring the men and women of the FBI a headquarters that meets their mission and their needs. After a years-long, competitive, and transparent process, Greenbelt, Maryland, was selected as the site for that new headquarters, based on its merits – including its ability to provide a secure space for the Bureau while ensuring the cost-effective use of taxpayer dollars. The Trump Administration had no grounds to ignore this selection, or redirect even one penny that Congress specifically appropriated for construction of the competitively selected site. We’re glad to see the Court acknowledge this fact, ruling that the Trump Administration’s actions are unlawful and void. This is an important step forward for the rule of law. This process began in 2009, and it’s past time it was concluded. Hopefully, the Trump Administration will agree with the conclusion that the Congress, the General Services Administration, and the District Court have all found, which is that Greenbelt is the proper home of the FBI. We will not stop fighting to fulfill our promise to the men and women of the Bureau to deliver a new, secure headquarters in Maryland so they can do their work without compromising their safety or our national security.”
title: Maryland Delegation Members’ Statement on State’s Victory in Lawsuit to Restore Greenbelt FBI Headquarters

U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), a senior member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, announced $4,609,282.00 in new federal funding for the San Luis Obispo County Airport for a range of infrastructure upgrades. Specifically, the funding will go towards modernizing Runway 11/29’s safety system, upgrading Taxiway A, and creating a plan to identify wildlife around the airport and assess how to protect aircraft from potential wildlife hazards, such as bird strikes.

“As SLO County continues to welcome more visitors each year, it’s essential that we invest in our local airport to maintain the highest levels of safety for passengers and crew,” said Rep. Carbajal. This $4.6 million federal investment will allow SLO County Airport to launch important infrastructure upgrades to enhance the overall travel experience.”

“We are deeply grateful to Congressman Carbajal and the U.S. Department of Transportation for this important investment, which will strengthen our airport, support our regional economy and help ensure San Luis Obispo County has the infrastructure needed to thrive for generations to come,” said San Luis Obispo County 3rd District Supervisor Dawn Ortiz-Legg.
title: Carbajal Announces $4.6 Million in New Federal Funding for SLO Airport

text:
West Springfield, MA — On Tuesday, August 18, Congressman Richard E. Neal joined West Springfield Mayor Will Reichelt, city councilors, and local officials to highlight the impact of federal investments made possible by the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). More than $1.5 billion has been invested across the First Congressional District.

In West Springfield, nearly $100 million was invested in projects and initiatives, with funding streams including:

$39.4 million in funding from the ARPA, consisting of $8.5 million in Coronavirus Local Fiscal Recovery funding and $30.9 million in Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief III funding.

$60 million in funding from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act

“When you consider what House Democrats were able to accomplish in just four years, it is truly quite remarkable. The three legislative achievements we are highlighting on this tour are certainly among the most consequential that I’ve been a part of during my career. With those dollars now having been put into action, I think it’s important that we take the time to take stock of these investments and inform the public as to what we’ve been able to accomplish,” said Congressman Neal. “I am pleased to join with Mayor Reichelt and members of the West Springfield City Council, all of whom have done a terrific job investing these federal dollars. Whether it be improvements to the Town’s infrastructure, issuing grants to local nonprofits and businesses, or enhancing public safety, West Springfield demonstrated what an effective partnership with the federal government should look like. I have no doubt that the residents will see the benefits of these investments for years to come.”

As a result of the ARPA, the Town of West Springfield was able to invest in its infrastructure, parks and recreation, public safety, community organizations, small-business recovery, municipal facilities, technology, and resident services. Projects supported by ARPA funds include:

$1.13 million towards transportation and pedestrian improvements, including:

The Piper Road/Amostown Road intersection

The Piper Road Complete Streets/Road Diet project

The Dewey Street sidewalks

The South Boulevard/Park Street/River Street intersection

Complete Streets sidewalk improvements

Kings Highway

$249,200 for the design work of the Route 5 water main

$2.8 million towards park and school improvements, such as:

$1 million for the Middle School track and improvements to the Middle School athletic fields

$514,000 for the Memorial Pool Splash Pad

More than $620,000 for townwide playground equipment and ground-cover improvements.

Additional funding also supported tennis courts, tree planting and maintenance, park entrances, the East-West Bike Trail Study, greenhouse and tree nursery improvements, and other recreational and environmental projects.

Investments in public safety, including:

$856,000 towards the Town’s consolidated emergency dispatch initiative

Additional funding supported firefighter turnout gear and emergency call boxes, as well as Police Department equipment, dispatch improvements, police bicycles and e-bikes, and start-up equipment for Animal Control.

Investments in community organizations and businesses that serve West Springfield residents, including $746,000 to nonprofit and community organizations, such as the West Springfield Boys & Girls Club, the Irish Cultural Center, the Eastern States Exposition/Hooplandia, the Tatham Club, and Friends of the Springfield Veterans Center.

Investments in municipal and school facility needs, including $648,000 towards improvements to the Municipal Office Building, Council on Aging, Police Department, school buildings, Morgan Road pavilion, and other Town facilities.

Investments in technology and municipal modernization, including $741,000 towards municipal fiber infrastructure and additional funding for Police Department software upgrades and municipal record digitization.

“We approached ARPA as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to make investments that would have a lasting impact on West Springfield,” said Mayor Reichelt. “These funds allowed us to take on major projects like our consolidated dispatch center, the Middle School track and the Memorial Pool splash pad while preserving local resources for other important needs. The result is stronger public safety, better community facilities and infrastructure that will serve our residents for years to come.”

In addition to the ARPA, MassDOT has received nearly $60 million from the IIJA and the IRA to support infrastructure projects that will benefit the Town of West Springfield, including:

The rehabilitation of Route 5 (Riverdale Road) from I-91 to Main Street in Holyoke and from Elm Street to North Elm Street in West Springfield

Pavement and bridge preservation on I-91

The Town also received a $198,603 grant through the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection, funded by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s Emerging Contaminants for Small or Disadvantaged Communities program. The funding supports a Granular Activated Carbon Pilot Study for the Southwick Wellfield treatment facility. This project will assist the Town in evaluating treatment strategies for emerging contaminants to ensure the continued safety, reliability, and resiliency of West Springfield’s drinking-water infrastructure.

###
title: Neal Makes First Stop on “Landmark Laws, Local Investments” Tour with Visit to West Springfield

SALINAS, CA — Today, Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren (CA-18) announced that Monterey County has received $250,000 from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) through the Preventing Violence Affecting Young Lives (PREVAYL) funding opportunity. This grant will be used to extend the Monterey County Health Department’s STRYVE Program for another year, which implements evidence-based approaches to prevent youth violence.

“One of my top priorities in Congress is ensuring that our communities are secure and healthy places to live and raise a family,” said Rep. Lofgren. “I am very glad to see that Monterey County is receiving this federal funding that will be used to continue its youth violence prevention efforts. The data shows that we’re making progress, but there is still work to be done, and we need to continue creating an environment where young people feel safe."

"As a longtime partner of the Community Alliance for Safety and Peace (CASP), I've been deeply invested in violence prevention work in Salinas, and proud of our results that show we are successfully keeping our children safe,” said Wendy Root Askew, Chair of the Monterey County Board of Supervisors. "We are grateful to have the strong support of Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren who secured funds needed to continue this critical work.”

The PREVAYL program is administered by the National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (NCIPC), which is part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The Monterey County Health Department began its STRYVE (Striving to Reduce Youth Violence Everywhere) Program in 2011, making it one of only four public health departments in the country to receive this funding. Since the start of this program, Monterey County went from having the highest levels of youth violence in California to seeing declining juvenile arrests and violent assaults of youth aged 10-24.

The funding will support youth violence prevention initiatives including:

Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) in schools, where students help identify environmental conditions that contribute to safety concerns and develop strategies to improve those spaces and student social cohesion

That’s Not Cool, a social media and youth engagement campaign developed by Futures Without Violence to prevent teen dating violence and intimate partner violence

Staff support for the continued development of a countywide violence prevention strategic plan, including coordination with community partners and alignment of state violence prevention efforts

Funded activities are currently focused primarily on the 93905 and 93906 ZIP codes in Salinas, which were identified as priority areas based on violence and health data.

title: Lofgren Announces $250k Federal Grant to Prevent Youth Violence in Monterey County

Lake Oswego, OR – Yesterday, U.S. Representative Andrea Salinas (OR-06) introduced the Lifeline for First Responders Act at a press conference hosted by Tualatin Valley Fire & Rescue (TVF&R) at Station 39. The bipartisan bill, which is co-led by Reps. Gabe Evans (CO-08), Sharice Davids (KS-03), and Thomas Kean Jr. (NJ-07), would create the first federal grant program dedicated to mental health care for firefighters, paramedics, and dispatchers, addressing a gap in support that first responders have faced for years.

"This has been Oregon's most devastating wildfire season on record. Our firefighters and paramedics have felt every bit of it. Just as we ask our first responders to be there for us, we need to be there for them,” said Rep. Salinas. “Up to a quarter of firefighters suffer from PTSD, and 37 percent of fire and EMS professionals have contemplated suicide, yet there is no federal program to address it, the way there is for law enforcement. My bill changes that. I'm proud to introduce the Lifeline for First Responders Act with the support of Tualatin Valley Fire and Rescue and NAMI Oregon to ensure our emergency personnel get the support they deserve.”

“As a former law enforcement officer, I know firsthand the toll that serving on the front lines can take on our first responders and emergency personnel. For too long, stigma has kept too many of our nation’s heroes from seeking the support they need. I’m proud to co-lead the Lifeline for First Responders Act to help break down those barriers and ensure the men and women who answer the call for us every day have access to the mental health resources, peer support, and confidential care they deserve,” said Rep. Evans.

“Firefighters and EMS professionals in Kansas and across the country can face more accidents, injuries, and tragedy in a single shift than most of us will experience in a lifetime. But too often, we treat their mental health as an afterthought. This bipartisan effort would make long-overdue investments in mental health services for first responders and make sure they know they don’t have to struggle in silence,” said Rep. Davids.

"Emergency medical professionals sacrifice so much to serve our communities. This bill would provide critical access to mental health support for those on the front lines who are at risk of higher rates of trauma and mental health struggles than the general population. Ensuring they have the resources they need will strengthen the safety and well-being of both those in EMS agencies and the communities they serve," said Rep. Kean.

Every day, first responders witness accidents, injuries, and devastation. That exposure can lead to burnout, PTSD, depression, and anxiety. Up to a quarter of firefighters suffer from PTSD, and 37 percent of fire and EMS professionals have contemplated suicide. In 2018, Congress recognized this need for law enforcement, authorizing the Law Enforcement Mental Health and Wellness Act to fund mental health prevention and treatment programs for police. No comparable program currently exists for fire and EMS personnel. The Lifeline for First Responders Act would close that gap.

Specifically, this bill would:

Establish a new EMS and First Responder Wellness Grant Program at the Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, through its Office of Emergency Medical Services;

Authorize $7.5 million a year, through fiscal year 2032, to fund evidence-based mental health and wellness services for fire, EMS, and dispatch personnel;

Fund suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention services, along with confidential counseling, peer support, and behavioral health care;

Fund family support services for the spouses and children of first responders; and

Fund outreach, stigma reduction, education, training, and technical assistance for fire departments, EMS agencies, and 911 dispatch centers building their own wellness programs.

"This is about the people who show up on your worst day and take care of your loved ones; it's time we show up for them and do the same. Talking about the struggles we all face is important; it's time to go beyond talking and make this a priority," said Deputy Chief Patrick Fale.

"First responders experience repeated exposure to trauma, yet too often face barriers to accessing the mental health care and support they need," said Michael Linskey, Director of Congressional Affairs at the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI). "NAMI is grateful to Representatives Salinas, Evans, Kean and Davids for introducing the Lifeline for First Responders Act, which invests in evidence-based mental health services, suicide prevention, peer support, and family resources. Supporting the mental health of those who protect our communities is critical to ensuring they can continue serving safely and effectively."

“First responders face significant occupational stressors, including repeated exposure to trauma, demanding shift schedules, and high-pressure work environments, all of which can increase suicide risk,” said Laurel Stine, J.D., M.A., Executive Vice President and Chief Policy and Advocacy Officer at the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP). “AFSP is proud to support the bipartisan Lifeline for First Responders Act, which would establish a dedicated grant program to expand access to evidence-based mental health and suicide prevention services for emergency personnel. By investing in workforce wellness, strengthening access to care, and reducing barriers to seeking support, this legislation would ensure first responders have the resources they need to protect their mental health. We thank Representatives Salinas, Evans, Kean and Davids for their bipartisan leadership in introducing this important legislation.”

Rep. Salinas introduced the bill in the House alongside Representatives Gabe Evans (CO-08), Thomas Kean Jr. (NJ-07), and Sharice Davids (KS-03). Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) are leading companion legislation in the Senate.

The Lifeline for First Responders Act is endorsed by Tualatin Valley Fire & Rescue, the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), the International Association of Fire Chiefs, the International Association of Fire Fighters, the National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians, Western Fire Chiefs Association, National Fallen Firefighters Foundation, the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, the Rhode Island Association of Fire Chiefs, and the Rhode Island State Association of Fire Fighters.

Letter questions whether the easing of human rights penalties was a concession to the PRC in trade negotiations
Washington, DC -- Today, Representatives Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, James P. McGovern (D-MA), Ranking Member of the House Rules Committee and Ranking Member of the Congressional-Commission on China, and Ro Khanna, Ranking Member of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and six other House Members sent a letter to President Trump expressing serious concern about his decision to allow an Executive Order to lapse. The decision resulted in sanctions relief for Chinese and Hong Kong officials complicit in Beijing’s dismantling of Hong Kong’s autonomy.
In his first term, President Trump issued Executive Order 13936 to employ emergency authorities to strip Hong Kong of its preferential trade and export-control treatment it had previously enjoyed as a distinct customs territory and authorize sanctions against individuals. In July 2026, President Trump declined to renew the Executive Order, thereby lifting sanctions on key individuals and sending a signal that the loss of Hong Kong’s autonomy is no longer a major concern for the U.S. government.
“We are also concerned about the circumstances surrounding this decision. The PRC’s Ministry of Commerce has publicly stated that the non-renewal implements understandings reached during the U.S.-PRC economic and trade consultations in Madrid, and that the United States made commitments concerning Hong Kong and investment-related issues during those talks,” wrote the Members of Congress. “If accurate, this would mean that sanctions relief for officials responsible for prosecuting pro-democracy activists was used as a bargaining chip in unrelated trade negotiations.”
The Members requested answers from the president about the decision, including justification for easing sanctions on complicit individuals, whether the decision was part of any quid-pro-quo with PRC officials, and whether the administration is committed to securing the release of publisher and prominent pro-democracy activist Jimmy Lai.
title: Meeks, McGovern, and Khanna Lead Colleagues in Demanding the Trump Administration Explain Decision to Lift Sanctions on Chinese and Hong Kong Officials

The bipartisan Accelerating Access to Dementia and Alzheimer’s Provider Training Act, or AADAPT Act, cosponsored by Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01) passed the House last month.

The legislation strengthens and reauthorizes the Project ECHO program to help primary care providers better identify, diagnose, and manage Alzheimer's disease and other dementias—particularly in rural and underserved communities.

“The AADAPT Act will help primary care providers diagnose Alzheimer’s and other dementias and ensure they feel prepared to deliver the care patients need. I’m proud to stand with families and advocates in support of this legislation, which has now passed the House,” said Congressman Pappas. “We must continue to raise awareness, support individuals, families, and caregivers, and fight to advance research, treatment, and care.”

“New treatments and new diagnostic tools are transforming what is possible for people living with Alzheimer’s,” said Robert Egge, Alzheimer’s Association chief public policy officer and AIM president. “The AADAPT Act ensures that primary care providers across the country — especially in rural and underserved communities — have the resources they need to bring that progress to their patients. We thank the bipartisan champions of this legislation for helping make that possible.”

More than 7 million Americans—including 27,000 Granite Staters—are living with Alzheimer's disease, and those numbers are expected to continue rising in the coming years. Because primary care providers are often the first health care professionals patients see when memory loss or cognitive decline begins, expanding access to specialized training can help improve early diagnosis and patient outcomes.

The AADAPT Act reauthorizes and strengthens the Project ECHO program, which connects primary care providers with specialists through virtual training, mentorship, and case-based learning. The program helps equip providers with the knowledge and confidence to identify potential cognitive impairment earlier, improve care coordination, and expand access to quality dementia care in communities that may lack specialty providers.
title: PASSED HOUSE: Pappas-Backed AADAPT Act to Improve Early Alzheimer's Detection and Care

TEMPE – U.S. Representative Greg Stanton (AZ-04) joined retirees and community advocates from the Arizona Alliance for Retired Americans (AARA) for a roundtable marking four years since the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The discussion focused on how the landmark law has lowered prescription drug costs and solutions to healthcare expenses that continue to strain seniors’ budgets.

“Four years ago, I took on Big Pharma and fought to get legislation signed into law that would finally empower Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices for seniors. Today I proudly celebrate the progress we’ve made, alongside advocates like the AARA,” said Rep. Stanton. “I’ll keep fighting in Congress to expand these savings, strengthen Medicare, and make sure Arizonans can retire with dignity.”

Stanton strongly supported the Inflation Reduction Act, which made major changes to Medicare Part D and Part B to lower drug costs. The law established a $2,000 out-of-pocket cap, capped insulin costs at $35 per month, made recommended vaccines available at no cost for people with Medicare Part D, expanded low-income subsidies, and empowered Medicare to negotiate drug prices.

In Arizona’s Fourth Congressional District alone, approximately 26,000 Medicare beneficiaries saved a combined $6 million on their prescriptions in 2024 because of the law’s drug pricing provisions. AZ-04 Constituent Doug Hart, who has been on Medicare for 15 years, shared during the roundtable how the IRA has helped him save up to $5,000 a year in out-of-pocket drug costs.

“Prescription drug costs are one of the biggest financial pressures facing older Arizonans, and no senior should have to choose between filling a prescription and paying for groceries, housing, or utilities," said Linda Somo, President of the Arizona Alliance for Retired Americans. "The Inflation Reduction Act took historic steps to lower those costs by finally giving Medicare the power to negotiate lower prices with drug companies and by capping what people with Medicare have to pay out of pocket for their prescriptions. These protections are already making a real difference for retirees living on fixed incomes. We need to build on this progress and make prescription drugs more affordable for all of us."
title: Stanton Celebrates Four Years of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Alongside Arizona Retirees
